The responsa of the Gaon Rav Shlomo Goren zt"l, in summarised form, were published under my editing in the bulletins of the Rabbis of Yesha (Judea, Samaria and Gaza), with the numbers and dates that I shall note beside each responsum. Everything published in the bulletins was before Rav Goren at the time of its publication, and he gave his approval to my editing, both in the work of summarising and in the work of correcting the style. Generally, when there was a need to change the style for the sake of clarity, I would consult with him and settle the wording for publication. Here I bring the responsa in full, and not as they were summarised or shortened in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin for lack of space. This responsum and the one after it, because of their length, were not printed in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin, except for what is printed below in siman 3, which is part of the second responsum.

Before each responsum published here I shall set out, in a different typeface, the background to its writing.

The first responsum, which is the longest of all, was indeed already published in 'Torat Ha-Medina', pages 114-134. However, since this responsum was first sent to me, and I hold its original text, and besides this, following its receipt I asked four further questions connected to it, I decided to publish here both the first responsum in its entirety and the further responsa that complete it, and in this way the learner will receive a more detailed picture of his view on this subject.

It should be noted that Rav Goren would first write the Hebrew date and beneath it the civil date. Incidentally, many rabbis also used to do so, and so I saw in the letter of approbation of the rabbi of Jerusalem, Rav Shalom Mashash zt"l, brought in the book 'Yalkut Shemesh'. However, here I did not find it necessary to mention it, following the words of my teacher and master the Ratziya in 'Le-Netivot Yisrael' vol. 2, pp. 564-565 (Beit El edition).

sections.title_en: Siman 1 – The Halakhic Status of Judea, Samaria and the Gaza Region
sections.body_en:
On 9 Marḥeshvan 5753, when I was secretary of the Rabbis of Yesha and editor of the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin, I sent a number of questions of principle to Rav Goren. In general I held that the main task of the rabbis of Israel is to define the changing reality according to the principles of the Torah, and for this purpose I asked these questions:

• What is the definition of the prohibition to hand over parts of Judea or Samaria to gentiles, and to what extent must one struggle against such a possibility?
• Is autonomy like handing over parts of the Land to foreigners, or is granting autonomy to the Arabs less severe? And must one take into account the clear danger that autonomy will develop into an Arab state, God forbid?
• Following voices heard in the media, there are residents who asked: what must a Jewish settler do if Jewish soldiers, or soldiers who are not Jewish, order him to leave his home, and threaten him that if he does not leave his home they will shoot him dead?

With God's help, 19 Marḥeshvan 5753

To the honourable Rav Eliezer Melamed

Rabbi of "Har Bracha" – Secretariat of the Rabbis of Yesha

May your peace be abundant.

I confirm receipt of your letter of 9 Marḥeshvan 5753, in which you ask to clarify, in the name of the Rabbis of Yesha, three fundamental problems concerning our status, our right and our duty in the regions of Judea and Samaria according to halakha. Although you did not mention the Gaza Strip in this context, I shall try in my response to refer also to Gaza and her towns. And I shall answer your questions, the first first.

Enclosed herewith is my detailed answer to the questions. In accordance with your request, I also attach a short summary of my answer on an additional page, in which all the sub-headings of my detailed answers are gathered, from which anyone can understand the content of the discussion of the responsum and the conclusions drawn from it.

Likewise I repeat on that page your questions, so that the reader may run through it and understand what is being discussed.

I hope that I have fulfilled your request in this answer, and if further problems arise for you, or objections to my words, please write them to me and I shall try to respond to your requests.

The one who writes and signs with every seal of blessing,
and with the blessing "This is the land which you shall inherit."

Rav Shlomo Goren

Summary of the Responsum

To question 1: (a) The mitzva of settling the Land of Israel has two applications: one applies to the person of Israel, and the second applies to the Land. (b) The holiness of the Land depends on the Jewish settlement in it. (c) Jewish sovereignty, and not settlement, determines whether the Land of Israel is built or destroyed. (d) The halakhic status of Judea, Samaria and the Gaza region under the rule of IDF occupation.
(e) It was forbidden by Torah law to leave Yesha outside Israeli sovereignty.
(f) The oaths with which the Holy One, blessed be He, adjured Israel not to go up as a wall and not to rebel against the nations have lost their force. (g) The renunciation by the Government of Israel of Israeli sovereignty in Yesha has no halakhic validity. (h) For three reasons it is impossible to grant the Arabs of Yesha the status of ger toshav (resident alien) so that they should have rights in the Land. (i) There is a Torah prohibition in giving up areas of the Land of Israel in Judea, Samaria and the Gaza region. (j) The possession of the Patriarchs in the Land was not only by virtue of the heavenly promise, but also by virtue of the conquest of the Land by Avraham our father from the hands of Kedorlaomer king of Elam, of the sons of Shem, and the kings with him. (k) In the two great wars, the War of Independence and the Six-Day War, we merited full sovereignty over the Land within the borders of the Bible. (l) According to the method of the Ra'avad and his school, it is possible to grant the Arabs of Yesha civil rights, but in no way to grant them national rights. (m) The mitzva of protest and rebuke against improper acts of the government is among the important mitzvot of the Torah. (n) There is no permission to use force or violence against the security forces in demonstrations of protest against the Jewish government.

To question 2: (o) Granting rights of autonomy to the Arabs involves a Torah prohibition according to the Rambam and also according to the Ra'avad. (p) Establishing a corporation of Arab cities, villages and settlements for the purpose of central self-governing municipal rule constitutes a halakhic problem. (q) There was never a Palestinian entity in the Land. Such an entity was created by the Prime Minister of Israel in the Camp David agreement.
(r) The Arabs of the Land of Israel have not, and never had, any national rights in the Land, but only a civil right of residence.

To question 3: (s) A strange question about a reality that will never occur in the Land, and therefore it is not fitting to discuss it in our house of study. (t) Summary – there are six messianic functions. (u) Everything that has happened and is happening in the Land is directed by a heavenly plan aimed at realising the vision of the third redemption.

The Full Responsum

(a) The mitzva of settling the Land of Israel has two applications: one applies to the person of Israel, and the second applies to the Land.1

Question 1: What is the definition of the prohibition to hand over parts of Judea or Samaria to gentiles, and to what extent must one struggle against such a possibility?

Answer: The mitzva of settling the Land of Israel is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah, as we learned in the Tosefta Avoda Zara (4:3): "This teaches that dwelling in the Land of Israel is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah." And in the Sifrei of the house of Rav on parashat Re'eh (piska 80), on the verse "and you shall dispossess them and dwell in their land" (Devarim 12:29), they said: "Dwelling in the Land of Israel is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah." It is not only a personal obligation of every Jew, who is obligated to live in the Land and fulfil the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel; rather it applies also to the Land of Israel itself, that the whole Land of Israel must be settled by Jews.

These two applications of the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel, one as a personal obligation and the second as an obligation of the Land, we learn from the two sources mentioned above in which this halakha appears. For in the Tosefta Avoda Zara mentioned above, the subject is the personal obligation to live in the Land of Israel, as we learned there: "A person should dwell in the Land of Israel, even in a city whose majority are gentiles, and not outside the Land, even in a city whose majority are Israel; this teaches that dwelling in the Land of Israel is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah, and whoever is buried in the Land of Israel, it is as though he were buried beneath the altar." This is a matter learned from its context: there the subject is the mitzva placed on the person of Israel as a personal obligation to live in the Land, just as it is a mitzva to be buried in the Land. Here the mitzva and the merit apply to the person and not to the soil, for there is no mitzva at all on the soil of the Land of Israel that Jews should be buried in it. On the contrary, from the point of view of the soil it is better that they not be buried in it, as we find in the Yerushalmi Kilayim (end of 9:4): "Rabbi Bar Kurya and Rabbi La'zar were walking in Istrin; they saw coffins coming from outside the Land. Rabbi Bar Kurya said to Rabbi La'zar: What have these accomplished? I apply to them (Yirmeyahu 2:7) 'and you made My inheritance an abomination' – in your lives; 'and you came and defiled My land' – in your deaths." This implies that there is no mitzva on the soil that Israel should be buried in it. So too with regard to the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel: the supreme importance is to live in the Land of Israel, and from this aspect it is a mitzva placed on the person.

On the other hand, from the words of the Sifrei mentioned above, which derives this halakha, that the mitzva of dwelling in the Land of Israel is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah, from the verse "and you shall possess it and dwell in it. And you shall take care to do all the statutes" (Devarim 11:31-32), this mitzva applies to the Land. For it is a mitzva on the Land of Israel that it be settled by Israel, since the holiness of the Land depends on the Jewish settlement in it, and every place that has been emptied of Jewish settlement has lost its holiness. As the Tosafot wrote in tractate Ketubot (45b, s.v. 'al'), where the Ri wrote: "For a city whose majority are idolaters, the holiness of the encircling wall is nullified. The wall is as though it did not exist; for from walled cities lepers are sent out, as we say in tractate Kelim (1:7), and when its majority are idolaters they are not sent out, because the holiness of the wall is nullified." So far the words of the Tosafot. We learn from their words that the holiness of walled cities depends on the Jewish settlement in them. And not only the holiness of walled cities, but also the holiness of the Land with regard to the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot depends on the Jewish settlement in it. As the Rambam wrote in chapter 1 of the Laws of Terumot, halakha 26: "For there is no Torah-law teruma except in the Land of Israel alone, and at a time when all Israel are there, as it is said: 'When you come' – the coming of all of you, as when they were in the first possession, and as they are destined to return in the third possession; not as when they were in the second possession, which was in the days of Ezra, which was the coming of only some of them, and therefore it did not obligate them by Torah law." So far his words. From here we see that the mitzva of settling the Land is also a mitzva dependent on the Land, which must be settled by Jews, for otherwise the holiness of the Land is not in it. That is to say, Jewish settlement and the holiness of the Land are bound up with and conditional on one another.

(b) The holiness of the Land depends on the Jewish settlement in it.

So it is implied from the derasha of the Sifrei on parashat Ekev (piska 51) on the verse (Devarim 11:24): "Every place on which the sole of your foot shall tread shall be yours." The Sifrei asks: "Or is it perhaps only that they have permission to conquer outside the Land before they conquer the Land? The verse teaches (Devarim 11:23): 'and you shall dispossess nations greater and mightier than you', and afterwards 'every place on which the sole of your foot shall tread shall be yours', so that the Land of Israel should not be defiled by their idols while you go back and conquer outside the Land." We learn from this that the mitzva is on the Land of Israel, that it be conquered and settled by Israel. And so it is implied from the words of the Ramban in the fourth mitzva that he adds to the positive commandments of the Rambam, where he wrote concerning the mitzva of destroying the seven nations "that we were commanded to kill those nations when they fight against us, and if they wished to make peace we make peace and leave them on known conditions. But the Land we shall not leave in their hands, nor in the hands of any other of the nations, in any generation." This implies that it is a mitzva placed on the Land, that we not leave it in the hands of foreigners, and it is part of the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel, which is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah, learned from the juxtaposition of the verses (Devarim 11:31-32): "and you shall possess it and dwell in it" and "you shall take care to do all the statutes and the judgements."

(c) Jewish sovereignty, and not settlement, determines whether the Land of Israel is built or destroyed.

Now, with regard to the building of the Land and its destruction, we have proofs that the matter does not depend on the Jewish settlement in it, but on the Jewish sovereignty over it. For the Magen Avraham writes (OḤ 561:1) on the words of the Shulḥan Arukh: "One who sees the cities of Yehuda in their destruction says, 'Your holy cities have become a wilderness', and tears." And the Magen Avraham writes there: "In their destruction – even though Israel dwell in them, since the nations rule over them it is called destruction." The Baḥ in his commentary on the Tur (OḤ 561, at the end of s.v. 'ha-ro'eh') brings a proof for this halakha of the Magen Avraham, and so the Baḥ writes there: "And it is simple that these cities of Yehuda in their destruction that are mentioned means even if there is settlement there; whatever the hand of the nations rules over is called in their destruction. For Mitzpa (Yirmeyahu 41:5), over which they tore, had there a settlement of many people of the Jews and Chaldean men of war. For they did not yet know that Gedalya had been killed and all the Jews who were in the fortress, and nevertheless they tore their garments because it was conquered under the hand of the king of Babylon." So far the words of the Baḥ. This is the method of the Baḥ and the Magen Avraham.

By contrast, the Beit Yosef is in doubt about this problem: is the intention the destruction of its settlement, but if there is settlement there, even if the gentiles rule there, it is called in its built state; or perhaps the matter does not depend on the existence of settlement in the place, but on the Jewish or foreign rule in the place. Although the language of the Beit Yosef in this is obscure and it is hard to reach the depth of his intention. For the Beit Yosef wrote there: "And these cities of Yehuda in their destruction that are mentioned means that they are ruined and have no settlement at all; but if there is settlement in them, even though they are in the hands of idolaters, it would seem at first sight that one need not tear. And it is possible that whatever is in the hands of idolaters, even though there is settlement in them, is called in their destruction, and this is the main view." And since the Beit Yosef too decides in the end that the latter method is the main one, one must accept this as a halakhic ruling from the mouths of the three pillars of instruction, the Beit Yosef, the Baḥ and the Magen Avraham, that everything depends on the rule in the place. If it is Jewish, even though there is no Jewish settlement there, the place is called in its built state; and if the rule is of foreigners, it is considered ruined and is called in its destruction. And although from the words of the Tosafot in tractate Ketubot mentioned above it is not implied so, as we wrote above that every city whose majority are idolaters has lost the holiness of walled cities, which implies that the matter depends on the Jewish settlement in it and not on Jewish sovereignty; but since the three great poskim, by whose mouths we live and from whose waters we drink, are of one view, that the building and destruction of the city depend on the rule in it, one must follow them.

(d) The halakhic status of Judea, Samaria and the Gaza region under the rule of IDF occupation.

Now we must clarify what the status of Judea, Samaria and the Gaza Strip is in light of the above halakha. Is the rule of the IDF in them considered Jewish rule, since the IDF rules there in terms of national and international law, and consequently these areas stand under Israeli sovereignty, the control over them being seemingly Jewish? Or perhaps, since neither Israeli law, neither secular nor halakhic, was applied to these areas, but rather Jordanian law remained in force in Judea and Samaria, and the status of the IDF in these areas, officially, both in terms of international law and in terms of Israeli law, is the status of a foreign occupier, as the Supreme Court of the State determined at the time in law and in practice; and all the authority, status and validity of the IDF in Yesha is by virtue of an occupier, according to the international convention. And not only that, but it turns out that the IDF never intended to conquer Yesha for Israel in order to annex them to the State, but in order to be there as responsible for providing the living conditions of the Arab population and their security. In such a situation Yesha were never placed under Jewish sovereignty, for from the outset the Government of Israel did not intend to conquer them in order that we should have ownership over them, but as a temporary guardian of the place.

According to this, it is possible that there is no meaning to the question of what the definition of the prohibition to hand over parts of Judea or Samaria to gentiles is, since we never received ownership or sovereignty over them. And although the IDF rules there, this is not by virtue of the ownership of a sovereign government over the area, which is what the Beit Yosef, the Baḥ and the Magen Avraham mentioned above intended in their words, but as an international guardian over these territories.

(e) It was forbidden by Torah law to leave Yesha outside Israeli sovereignty.

However, here is the difficulty: according to the halakha established by the Ramban mentioned above, it was forbidden to leave Yesha outside Jewish sovereignty. And every single day that we do not join Judea, Samaria and the Gaza region to the sanctified Land of Israel under Israeli sovereignty, we transgress a positive commandment of the Torah, in which we were commanded "to inherit the Land that God, may He be exalted, gave to our fathers, to Avraham, to Yitzḥak and to Ya'akov, and not to leave it in the hands of others of the nations or to desolation, and this is what He said: 'And you shall possess the land and dwell in it, for to you I have given the land to possess it.'" And the Ramban further wrote there: "But the Land we shall not leave in their hands nor in the hands of any other of the nations in any generation. And likewise, after we have cut off the peoples, if our tribes wished to leave it and conquer for themselves the land of Shinar or the land of Ashur or other places, they are not permitted, for we were commanded concerning its conquest and settlement." This is the method of the Ramban, according to which the Government of Israel transgresses this mitzva every single day, in that we have not annexed Yesha to the State of Israel and have not applied Israeli law to it.

Indeed, the Rambam disagrees with the Ramban and holds that there is no positive commandment of the Torah to conquer the Land of Israel in every generation, as the 'Megillat Esther' wrote there: "For the mitzva of inheriting the Land and settling it applied only in the days of Moshe and Yehoshua and David, and all the time that they had not gone into exile from their land; but after they went into exile from their land this mitzva does not apply for the generations until the time of the coming of the Messiah. For on the contrary, we were commanded, according to what they said at the end of Ketubot (111a), that we not rebel against the nations by going to conquer the Land as a wall."

But even according to the Rambam, following the explanation of the 'Megillat Esther', this is only before we conquered the Land in the War of Independence and in the Six-Day War, that in the view of the Rambam there is no mitzva for the generations to conquer the Land of Israel. But once we have already conquered it, because we were forced to do so on the basis of "helping Israel from an enemy who comes upon us", a situation that existed in the Six-Day War, which even in the view of the Rambam is an obligatory war, as he wrote in chapter 5 of the Laws of Kings, halakha 1; and afterwards there arose the problem of defending the Land that we liberated under the compulsion of the situation that then existed: it is reasonable to assume that even in the view of the Rambam we are forbidden now to abandon the Land that we conquered and acquired by conquest of war according to halakha, as will be clarified below, and it is our duty to defend it against every enemy and foe who plots to drive us out of our Land. For even according to the Rambam, although the conquest of the Land is not a mitzva, the defence of the Land of Israel that is in our hands is a mitzva of the Torah.

(f) The oaths with which the Holy One, blessed be He, adjured Israel not to go up as a wall and not to rebel against the nations have lost their force.

As for what the 'Megillat Esther' relies on, the passage of the Gemara at the end of Ketubot there: The Holy One, blessed be He, adjured Israel with three oaths: that they not go up as a wall and that they not rebel against the nations of the world, etc. – the divine kabbalist Rav Ḥayim Vital, may his merit protect us, the foremost disciple of the holy Ari, already wrote in his introduction to the book 'Etz Ḥayim' that the above oaths brought in tractate Ketubot were in force only until the end of the fifth millennium. But from then on, on the contrary, it is a mitzva to go up as a wall, to fight and struggle for the liberation of the Land of Israel and for the redemption of Israel.

Also in the letter of the Gaon Rabbi Meir Simḥa of Dvinsk zt"l, author of the 'Or Same'aḥ' on the Rambam, which he wrote after the Balfour Declaration, he rules that after the conference of the united nations in San Remo decided to adopt the Balfour Declaration and to guarantee the Jewish people the national home in the Land of Israel, the force of the above oaths, that Israel not go up as a wall and not rebel against the nations, lapsed, since the League of Nations gave its approval to our rights in the Land of Israel.

Now, although the IDF and the Civil Administration in Yesha operate according to international law, which sees the status of the IDF as a foreign occupier, and although the Government of Israel agreed and agrees to this day to this status of ours as a foreign occupier in Yesha,2 we are bound by Jewish halakha. And since according to halakha we ought to have realised the ownership and acquisition of the military conquest in the Six-Day War and declared Jewish sovereignty in Yesha, even if we did not do so, we must regard our halakhic status in the territories of Yesha as though we had applied to them the sovereignty of the State of Israel, since according to halakha conquest in war is a complete acquisition. As the Ḥiddushei Ha-Rashba proves in tractate Gittin 37b, s.v. 'shebe'i', that possession by war is a complete acquisition even of land, as the Gemara establishes there regarding an idolater who acquires by conquest in war, like Ammon and Moav, which were purified through Siḥon; all the more so Israel from idolaters.

Therefore, according to halakha, Israel's conquest in war in the Six Days is considered a complete acquisition that grants the people of Israel complete ownership over Yesha. And although the State and the IDF did not intend to acquire Yesha with a complete acquisition, but to operate there as a foreign occupier, the Government of Israel had no right by Torah law to give up our sovereignty over Yesha, where the essence and importance of the Land of Israel lie, and where the Lord commanded the blessing, life for ever.

(g) The renunciation by the Government of Israel of Israeli sovereignty in Yesha has no halakhic validity.

Consequently, the renunciation by the Government of Israel of Yesha as a sovereign area of the people of Israel has no halakhic validity, in light of the clear halakha in the Rambam, chapter 10, halakha 6 of the Laws of Idolatry: "All these things are said only at a time when Israel are exiled among the idolaters, or when the hand of the idolaters is strong over Israel. But at a time when the hand of Israel is strong over them, we are forbidden to leave idolaters among us. And even one who dwells temporarily, or passes from place to place with merchandise, shall not pass through our land until he accepts upon himself the seven mitzvot that the sons of Noaḥ were commanded, as it is said: 'They shall not dwell in your land' (Shemot 23:33), even for a time. And if he accepted upon himself seven mitzvot, he is a ger toshav. And one accepts a ger toshav only at a time when the Jubilee applies; but at a time when the Jubilee does not apply, one accepts only a righteous convert." And the Rambam in chapter 14 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations, halakha 7, rules: "Who is a ger toshav? This is an idolater who accepted upon himself not to worship stars and constellations, together with the other mitzvot that the sons of Noaḥ were commanded, and did not circumcise and did not immerse; such a one we accept, and he is of the pious of the nations of the world. And why is he called toshav (resident)? Because we are permitted to settle him among us in the Land of Israel." So far his words.

We thus learn from the mouth of the Rambam that if we do not grant the Arabs of Yesha the status of ger toshav [which we are not permitted to do, as will be explained below for several reasons], it is forbidden to leave them in the Land. And since from the Six-Day War onwards our hand became strong over them, in such a situation, in which we rule in the Land, it is forbidden according to the method of the Rambam, seemingly, to leave them in the Land. And there is a widespread halakha in Israel, explicit in tractate Temura (4b), where Rava said: "Anything about which the Merciful One said do not do it, if one did it, it has no effect at all." It follows that although the Government of Israel did not intend to apply Jewish ownership over Yesha, contrary to halakha, the government's decision in this matter has no halakhic validity, and the law of these areas is as being under Israeli sovereignty.3

(h) For three reasons it is impossible to grant the Arabs of Yesha the status of ger toshav so that they should have rights in the Land.

[1] The first reason is as the Rambam himself establishes in the Laws of Idolatry mentioned above and in chapter 14 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations, halakha 8: "And one accepts a ger toshav only at a time when the Jubilee applies; but in our time, even if he accepted upon himself the whole Torah except for one detail, we do not accept him." Indeed, the Ra'avad disagrees with the Rambam on this (in the Laws of Idolatry mentioned above) and writes in his glosses there, "Says Avraham: I do not agree with him regarding dwelling in the Land," that is, in the view of the Ra'avad, even in our time, whoever keeps the seven mitzvot that the sons of Noaḥ were commanded, although he is not accepted as a ger toshav officially, it is permitted to settle him in the Land. It is doubtful whether the Ra'avad decides the halakha against the method of the Rambam. In addition to this, even according to the Ra'avad, it is not in our power to grant the Arabs of Yesha the status of ger toshav, because of the reasons below.

[2] Even at a time when the Jubilee applies, it would not have been possible, according to the Rambam, to grant the status of ger toshav to the Arabs of Yesha. Although the Muslims are not idolaters, and they declare the unity of God, may He be exalted, as is fitting, a unity without blemish, as the Rambam establishes in his responsum to Rabbi Ovadya the convert in the new responsa of the Rambam, siman 448; nevertheless, those among them who lend a hand to the intifada are suspected of the murder of Jews, whether they do so in practice, or whether they know of it and are silent and do not fight against the terrorists and murderers. The law of both of these is as though they violate the mitzva "You shall not murder" and the mitzva of dinim (justice), which is one of the seven mitzvot that the sons of Noaḥ were commanded. For the Rambam holds in chapter 9 of the Laws of Kings, halakha 14 – since the sons of Noaḥ are commanded concerning dinim – "For this reason all the men of Shekhem were liable to death, for Shekhem robbed, and they saw and knew and did not judge him." The same law applies to the Arabs of Yesha who are members of the PLO or of another terrorist organisation, or who cooperate actively or passively with the murderers in the intifada, who see daily the attacks on soldiers and civilians on the part of hundreds of the residents. In every area in the territories stones are thrown by the children of the residents, and the responsibility is on the parents. It follows that a large part of the Arabs of the territories do not fulfil their obligation regarding the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ in everything relating to executing justice on criminals and murderers. And even those among them who are passive and do not cooperate with the terrorists, if their heart is with those who hold that the Land of Israel does not belong to the Jews, as the Torah of Israel obligates, one must not grant them the status of ger toshav in order to receive a right of dwelling in the Land.

As for them, whether they are a majority or whether they are a minority, even if there were not the restriction against granting them the status of ger toshav and allowing the dwelling of the Arabs of Yesha in the Land because the Jubilee does not apply, they do not keep the seven mitzvot that the sons of Noaḥ were commanded, which include not to steal and not to murder and not to rob, and to execute justice on criminals. Therefore, after the outbreak of the intifada, those who are suspected of cooperating with the terror organisations have no right of dwelling in the Land, according to the Rambam and the Ra'avad together.

[3] The third reason why it is impossible to grant the Arabs of Yesha the status of ger toshav is because the Rambam rules in chapter 8 of the Laws of Kings, halakha 11: "Whoever accepts upon himself the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ and is careful to do them, he is of the pious of the nations of the world and has a share in the world to come. And this is provided that he accepts them and does them because the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded them in the Torah and made known to us through Moshe our teacher that the sons of Noaḥ had been commanded them before. But if he did them because of the conclusion of reason, he is not a ger toshav, and he is not of the pious of the nations of the world nor of their wise men." So far his words.

Now the Arabs of Yesha, even one who has no hand in terror and is not suspected of giving help to the intifada, if they believe in the unity of God and keep the other mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ because they believe in the Quran and because Muhammad commanded them so, and not because of the command of Moshe our teacher to the sons of Noaḥ, because they believe that so Moshe our teacher was commanded on Mount Sinai – the law of ger toshav does not apply to them; they are not of the pious of the nations of the world nor of their wise men, and they have no share in the world to come.

Since the Ra'avad too does not disagree with this condition in the Rambam, and also does not disagree with his view regarding the obligation of keeping the mitzva of dinim, by virtue of which they are obligated to fight against the criminals among them, we learn that even according to the view of the Ra'avad, although it would have been possible to grant the status of ger toshav to those among the Arabs who keep the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ in our time, even when the Jubilee does not apply, as above, it is impossible to do so with regard to the Muslims among us.

(i) There is a Torah prohibition in giving up areas of the Land of Israel in Judea, Samaria and the Gaza region.

For the last two reasons it is forbidden to give up to the Arabs areas of the Land of Israel in Yesha too, because according to halakha we have ownership over all the territories of Yesha, even though the State and the IDF did not intend to apply the sovereignty of Israel over these areas. There is a Torah prohibition against concessions of territories of Yesha to the Arabs of the area; the prohibition is on account of "lo teḥonem" of the Torah, which the Sages explained as "do not give them a resting place (ḥaniya) in the land", as we learned in tractate Avoda Zara (20a), and in the Rambam, chapter 10 of the Laws of Idolatry, halakha 4.4

Now we have already explained in the book 'Torat Ha-Mo'adim', p. 627, that over every area of land, in every place in the world, there are two domains of ownership. One is the supreme domain of the government, by virtue of which it may impose taxes and rates on all the landowners; and the second is the private domain of the landowners, as private property. And wherever the supreme domain over the land is in the hands of the state, it is considered as ruling and sovereign over the land, as the Tosafot wrote in tractate Kiddushin (36b, s.v. 'kol'): "Therefore terumot and ma'asrot were nullified outside the Land, because now outside the Land the lands are not ours, for they are mortgaged to the king and we give tax from them to the king. If so, they do not have the law of land with regard to separating teruma and ma'aser. And if you will say: in the Land of Israel too the lands are mortgaged to the king, and nevertheless one separates teruma and ma'aser – one may say that an idolater has no acquisition in the Land of Israel to release it from ma'aser." So far the words of the Tosafot. And so we find in the Tosafot in tractate Bava Batra (55a, s.v. 'im'), who wrote: "But for the king's tax, even land worth a thousand zuz is mortgaged for a small thing, and the land is essentially the king's," etc. One may therefore learn from the words of the Tosafot in tractate Kiddushin mentioned above that in the Land of Israel a foreign king has no sovereignty over the lands, and therefore it is not in his power to release the holiness of the Land, because the Land of Israel is held by us from our fathers, as we find in tractate Bava Batra (119a) that the Land of Israel is a held possession and an inheritance to us from our fathers. And so it is explicit in the Yerushalmi Ḥalla (2:1): "There, before they entered it, they inherited retroactively, for Rav Huna said in the name of Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥman: 'To your seed I will give' is not written here, but 'To your seed I have given' – I have already given." This is the supreme ownership of the Jewish people over all the lands in the sanctified Land of Israel, which we inherited from our fathers.

(j) The possession of the Patriarchs in the Land was not only by virtue of the heavenly promise, but also by virtue of the conquest of the Land by Avraham our father from the hands of Kedorlaomer king of Elam, of the sons of Shem, and the kings with him.

Now we have already clarified that this supreme ownership too over the soil of the Land of Israel, which came to us seemingly from the Covenant between the Pieces, was not given to Avraham our father only by the hand of Heaven, through the retroactive promise, as it were, "To your seed I have given this land," etc. Rather, Avraham our father conquered the Land from the hands of Kedorlaomer king of Elam, who was of the sons of Shem, as it is written in Bereshit (10:22): "The sons of Shem: Elam," etc. And as Rashi wrote (there 14:18), that Avraham in his war against the four kings killed the sons of Shem, because Kedorlaomer king of Elam was of the sons of Shem.5 And after the Land of Israel fell in the world division to the sons of Shem, as it is written, "When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance, when He separated the children of man, He set the borders of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel" (Devarim 32:8), the Canaanites, of the sons of Ḥam, conquered the Land of Israel unlawfully from the sons of Shem, as it is written (there 10:6): "And the sons of Ḥam: Kush and Mitzrayim and Put and Kena'an," "And Kena'an begot Tzidon his firstborn, and Ḥet; and the Yevusi and the Emori and the Girgashi" (there 15-16), "And the border of the Canaanite was from Tzidon, as you come to Gerar, to Aza; as you come to Sedom and Amora and Adma and Tzevoyim, to Lasha" (there 19). And so Rashi wrote (there 12:6): "'And the Canaanite was then in the land' – he was going on and conquering the Land of Israel from the seed of Shem, for it had fallen to the portion of Shem when Noaḥ divided the earth among his sons, as it is said (there 14:18): 'And Malki-Tzedek king of Shalem.'"

Kedorlaomer, of the sons of Shem, at first fought against the domination of the Canaanites in the Land and conquered parts of it back for the sons of Shem, as it is written (there 14:4-5): "Twelve years they served Kedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled. And in the fourteenth year Kedorlaomer came, and the kings that were with him," etc.

From the language of the verse it is clear that the initiative for this war against the Canaanites who had conquered the Land of Israel was Kedorlaomer's, and the kings who were with him came only to help Kedorlaomer, because he had the great interest in returning the Land that had fallen to the sons of Shem from the hands of the Canaanite conquerors. And so it is implied from the verse below (there 14:17): "And the king of Sedom went out to meet him after his return from smiting Kedorlaomer and the kings that were with him," implying that Kedorlaomer is the one who initiated this war, and he represented the sons of Shem in claiming ownership of the Land. And Malki-Tzedek too is Shem son of Noaḥ, as Rashi explained there (and so says the Targum Yonatan ben Uziel), who came in order to defend the right of the sons of Shem in the Land. And indeed Kedorlaomer, of the sons of Shem, defeated the five kings of Kena'an who had taken control of the Land. And the Land would have remained in his possession, as in the twelve years in which the people of Sedom and Amora served Kedorlaomer.

And then came Avraham, he too of the sons of Shem, but of the descendants of Ever, to whom the Holy One, blessed be He, promised ownership over the Land of Israel as the exclusive representative of the sons of Shem, and not to Kedorlaomer king of Elam; and he fought on behalf of the Canaanite rule that ruled in Sedom and Amora, Adma and Tzevoyim, as stated in the verse in parashat Noaḥ (10:19), against Kedorlaomer king of Elam, who saw himself as the representative of the sons of Shem. And Avraham conquered the Land back from the hands of Kedorlaomer king of Elam. And since conquest in war is an acquisition by Torah law, it follows that Avraham our father inherits the Land of Israel not only by virtue of the heavenly promise in the Covenant between the Pieces, but also by virtue of conquest in war. And in the negotiations between Avraham and the king of Sedom the Land was not spoken of at all, for Avraham never gave up his right of ownership in the Land of Israel. Rather, what was spoken of between them was the persons whom he returned from captivity and the property of Sedom and Amora that Kedorlaomer and his companions had plundered, as it is written (there 14:11), "And they took all the goods of Sedom and Amora and all their food, and went." In this Kedorlaomer king of Elam demonstrated the seizure of ownership by the sons of Shem over the Land of Israel from the hands of the Canaanites. And Avraham in turn conquered it from Kedorlaomer, even though he too was of the sons of Shem. And then it is written there (15:1): "After these things the word of the Lord came to Avram in a vision, saying," etc. And Rashi explained: "After this miracle was done for him, that he killed the kings." The meaning of the matter is that Avraham acquired the Land of Israel by conquest in war from the hands of Kedorlaomer. On the basis of this acquisition of the Land of Israel by Avraham in war, "On that day the Lord made a covenant with Avram, saying: To your seed I have given the land" (there 15:18). And He did not say to him "I will give", as the Holy One, blessed be He, had promised Avraham before the war (see Bereshit 12:7 and there 13:15-17), because Avraham had already gained the Land by conquest in war, and not only through the heavenly promise. For this reason the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him at the Covenant between the Pieces "to your seed I have given", because of the conquest of Avraham our father; and therefore the Gemara says (Bava Batra 111a) that the Land of Israel is held by them from their fathers.

(k) In the two great wars, the War of Independence and the Six-Day War, we merited full sovereignty over the Land within the borders of the Bible.

Let us return to the earlier matters. We have come to see that there are two kinds of acquisition in the Land: one is the supreme acquisition of the people and the state, and this is our sovereignty over the lands of the Land of Israel. This sovereignty is what determines the holiness of the Land of Israel, which the people gained at first as an inheritance from Avraham our father, and in the second exile we lost it. In our days, in the War of Independence and in the Six-Day War, we returned to ourselves national sovereignty over the Land, which is our supreme acquisition over the whole Land of Israel, within the biblical borders sanctified by those who came up from Egypt, and part of it by those who came up from Babylon. For whether according to the one who says that the holiness of the Land lapsed with the destruction of the Second Temple, or according to the one who says that its holiness did not lapse because the holiness of the Land of Israel was sanctified for its time and sanctified for the future to come, certainly the conquest of the Land by the IDF in the two wars together, in the War of Independence and in the Six-Day War, constitutes an acquisition and a taking of ownership over the whole Land. And we shall not leave it in the hands of strangers, as the Ramban wrote in his glosses on the Rambam's Book of Mitzvot.

Here we must distinguish the supreme acquisition of the people of Israel over the whole Land of Israel, including Judea, Samaria and the Gaza region, that, according to what was explained above, even if the State left Yesha under Jordanian law, and we left ourselves as foreign occupiers, as it were, this does not take effect from the point of view of halakha. For the moment we conquered it we gained supreme ownership over the whole Land of Israel, for it is a severe Torah prohibition to give up this supreme sovereignty.

It should be noted that no national or political body among the Arabs of the Land of Israel ever gained this sovereignty over the Land, nor any national rights in the Land of Israel. The Jordanians conquered Judea and Samaria in the War of Independence contrary to international law, for no international organisation granted them any right in Judea, in Samaria and in Jerusalem. Rather, Jordan annexed them to itself for nineteen years until the Six-Day War by virtue of conquest in war, for according to the halakha we mentioned above, explicit in tractate Gittin (38a) and in the Rashba there, gentiles too have acquisition through conquest in war.

(l) According to the method of the Ra'avad and his school, it is possible to grant the Arabs of Yesha individual civil rights, but in no way to grant them national rights.

Now when the IDF came after nineteen years and liberated Judea and Samaria from the hands of the Jordanians, no other Arab body gained a national right over these territories. For the Arabs of the Land of Israel never ruled here, and in the whole history of the Land of Israel they never gained any national rights or any sovereignty whatsoever in any part of the Land of Israel. What they can claim for themselves are private civil rights over their places of residence, without any national rights, for these rights were never granted to them by any national body that ever ruled in the Land of Israel.

This is if we ignore completely the method of the Rambam mentioned above, who forbade granting dwelling in the Land to non-Jews unless we grant the Arabs of the Land of Israel the status of ger toshav, and, as we have seen, this too is impossible. What we can agree to, contrary to the method of the Rambam, is to grant the residents of Judea and Samaria an individual civil right of residence in their villages, without granting any national rights. For national rights mean, according to halakha, giving them a resting place in the Land, which they did not have before. A private right of residence for those who were born here and continue to live here is understandable: we are not giving them a resting place in the Land; rather they gained it by inheritance and by their possession of the place of residence. But to grant them any national rights whatsoever, which never existed, is a transgression of "lo teḥonem", which means according to halakha "do not give them rights of resting in the land."

On the other hand, according to the method of the Ramban mentioned above, who holds that all the mitzvot and commands that we find in the Torah concerning the Land of Israel apply for the generations, the great mitzva in parashat Masei (Bamidbar 33:53), "And you shall dispossess the land and dwell in it, for to you I have given the land to possess it," obligates us today too. And because of the non-fulfilment of this mitzva there is being realised before our eyes the threat of the Torah: "But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those whom you let remain of them shall be as pricks in your eyes and as thorns in your sides, and they shall harass you in the land in which you dwell" (Bamidbar 33:55). To our sorrow this verse has been fulfilled in us exactly, according to the interpretation of Targum Onkelos on this verse: "And those whom you leave of them will be bands bearing weapons against you, and encampments surrounding you, and they will oppress you in the land in which you dwell." In this translation there is an exact description of the intifada of our time.

Thus far the answer to the first part of the first question.

(m) The mitzva of protest and rebuke against improper acts of the government is among the important mitzvot of the Torah.

As for the second part of your question 1, "to what extent must one struggle against such a possibility?" – if it were a matter of a foreign government coming to dispossess us of our inheritance, we would have a mitzva and a duty to give our lives in defence of the Land against strangers, as we have already clarified that the mitzva of conquering the Land according to the Ramban, and the defence of the Land also according to the Rambam, override the saving of life.6 But since it is a matter of a struggle against a Jewish government that is about to hand over parts of the Land of Israel to strangers, we are subject to the laws of protest and the mitzva of rebuke that are placed on every person of Israel, whether against an individual or against the many, or against the bearers of government, such as the king in the Land of Israel and the Exilarch in Babylon, which is considered a most important mitzva. For we find in tractate Shabbat (55a): "Rabbi Zeira said to Rabbi Simon: Let the master rebuke these of the house of the Exilarch. He said to him: They will not accept it from me. He said to him: Even though they will not accept it, let the master rebuke them, for Rabbi Aḥa son of Rabbi Ḥanina said: Never did a good measure go out from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, and He then retracted it for evil, except for this matter, as it is written (Yeḥezkel 9:4): 'And the Lord said to him: Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and who cry for all the abominations that are done in its midst,' etc. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Gavriel: Go and mark on the foreheads of the righteous a tav of ink, so that the angels of destruction shall not rule over them; and on the foreheads of the wicked a tav of blood, so that the angels of destruction shall rule over them. The attribute of justice said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the world, how are these different from those? He said to it: These are completely righteous, and those are completely wicked. It said before Him: Master of the world, it was in their power to protest, and they did not protest! He said to it: It is revealed and known before Me that if they had protested against them, they would not have accepted it from them. It said before Him: Master of the world, if it is revealed before You, to them who revealed it?! And this is what is written (there 9:6): 'Old man, young man and maiden, and little children and women, slay utterly… and begin at My sanctuary.' And it is written (there): 'And they began with the elders who were before the House,'" etc.

And so they said there in the Gemara (Shabbat 54b): "Whoever could have protested against the members of his household and did not protest is held responsible for the members of his household; against the people of his city, he is held responsible for the people of his city; against the whole world, he is held responsible for the whole world." And so the Rambam ruled in chapter 6 of the Laws of Character Traits, halakha 7. And in Sanhedrin (27b) they expounded the verse (Vayikra 26:37) "and they shall stumble one upon his brother": "one through the iniquity of his brother; this teaches that all are guarantors for one another, for it was in their power to protest and they did not protest." And see Yoreh De'a siman 157, that where there is a concern of danger to oneself through protest, one is not obligated even to spend his money on it.

(n) There is no permission to use force or violence against the security forces in demonstrations of protest against the Jewish government.

We thus learn that the severity of the mitzva of protest against the government is very great. And the responsibility lies in this: that the transgression against which he did not protest is charged to the one who did not protest enough. We must therefore exercise by all non-violent means the duty of protest that is in our hands against handing over territories of the Land of Israel to foreigners. For all the laws of rebuke against an individual, as it is written, "You shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him" (Vayikra 19:17), are in force also against the government and the public when they sin. Therefore in every obligatory struggle against a government acting contrary to the Torah of Israel, we are commanded to exercise all the means of rebuke and protest in our hands that do not require violence and the use of force against the security forces, according to the law of the mitzva of rebuke. As we learned in the Gemara in Arakhin (16b): "How far does rebuke go? Rav said: until striking; and Shmuel said: until cursing; and Rabbi Yoḥanan said: until reproach." And the Rambam in chapter 6 of the Laws of Character Traits, halakha 7, rules like Rav, for he wrote there: "And so a person is always obligated to rebuke him until the sinner strikes him and says to him: I will not listen."

It is implied from this halakha that on the part of the one rebuking and protesting there is no aspect of permission to use violence. Rather he is obligated to continue in protest and rebuke quietly until the sinner strikes him. And in our case the meaning is that he is obligated to go out and demonstrate against the government until the police use force against the demonstrators; and then it is forbidden to use counter-violence, but one must stop the demonstration in order to avoid bodily injuries from the police. And although these things are seemingly said concerning the rebuke of an individual against an individual, or the protest of the many against an individual or individuals, one can prove from the passage of the Gemara in Arakhin mentioned above that this halakha applies also in a dispute over political matters standing at the summit of the world. For the source of these differences of opinion between the above Amoraim is the quarrel that broke out between Shaul and Yehonatan (I Shmuel 20:31). There it is written: "And Shaul cast the spear at him to smite him," etc. The quarrel between Shaul and Yehonatan was over the future of the kingdom of Israel, when Shaul intended to kill David, who was destined to be the anointed of the Lord, and Yehonatan protested against this before King Shaul his father.

We learn from this that even in political matters standing at the summit of our world and our future, the force of these halakhot is firm and established. According to the one who says the mitzva of rebuke goes until striking, even against political transgressions it is forbidden for the demonstrator to use violence; and all the more so according to the one who says until cursing or until reproach, certainly there is no obligation to use force against the sinners. For this is the limit that obligates demonstrating and protesting against political plans of the government that involve a transgression of the laws of the Torah, and not beyond it. From this passage of tractate Arakhin it is implied that the limit "until striking" holds also in an irreversible case, that is, where after the political plan against which we wish to protest and demonstrate is carried out, it will be a crookedness that cannot be made straight. For in the case of Shaul and Yehonatan, had Shaul killed David, it would have been irreparable. And nevertheless the halakha sets this limit of not using violence and force on the part of those protesting and demonstrating.

Even if we compare handing over parts of the Land of Israel to foreigners to one who pursues his fellow to kill him, for which there is the prohibition "You shall not stand by the blood of your fellow", and one is obligated to save him at the cost of the pursuer's life – even there, wherever the rescuer must endanger his own life in saving his fellow, he is not obligated in this mitzva. And in the view of the poskim, even in doubtful danger to oneself one is exempt from saving his fellow, as the Radbaz ruled in a responsum (vol. 3, 625). And see the Pitḥei Teshuva (YD 157:15), that one who does not conduct himself so is called a pious fool. Except for the method of the Kesef Mishneh, who wrote in chapter 1 of the Laws of a Murderer and Preservation of Life in the name of the Yerushalmi, that in a case of doubtful danger to oneself in saving one's fellow, one is obligated to endanger oneself in doubt in order to save the other from certain danger to life, because the other's danger is certain and his is doubtful. It may be that in the case of handing over territories to foreigners, even the Kesef Mishneh would agree that one is not obligated to endanger one's life even in doubt. But we have no clear halakhic decision in this, since we have proved in several articles and with clear proofs that the defence of Israeli sovereignty in the sanctified territories of the Land of Israel overrides the saving of life; wherever there is a reasonable chance that through self-endangerment and self-sacrifice on our part we will prevent the handing over of the territories to a foreigner, perhaps one must act so according to halakha. But it is very hard to reach a clear halakhic conclusion in this, in light of the contradictory methods and the varied views on it; [therefore] one should not rule in halakha and in practice to give one's life in such a protest. Rather, as the halakha establishes regarding the mitzva of rebuke, we shall do our part according to the Torah and the mitzva, and fulfil our obligation by the rebuke and the demonstration that we hold against the policy of handing over territories of the Land of Israel to strangers, and the Lord will do what is good in His eyes.

(o) Granting rights of autonomy to the Arabs involves a Torah prohibition according to the Rambam and also according to the Ra'avad.

Question 2: "Is autonomy like handing over parts of the Land to foreigners, or is granting autonomy to the Arabs less severe? And must one take into account the clear danger that autonomy will develop into an Arab state, God forbid?"

Answer: Although we wrote above that granting municipal rights to the Arabs of the territories may involve the Torah prohibition of "lo teḥonem", this is only according to the method of the Rambam. But according to the Ra'avad in his glosses on the Rambam, it is possible to grant the Arabs of Yesha, to whoever is not a member of the PLO or of another terrorist organisation and does not cooperate with them, municipal rights over purely Arab cities and villages, that they should look after themselves, education, cleanliness, and keep the building laws of the State, and collect municipal taxes and the like, in each city and each village separately. Likewise they are permitted to establish for themselves a system of magistrates' courts to judge for themselves. For the derasha in the Gemara Kiddushin (76b), "You shall surely set a king over you… from among your brothers you shall set a king over you" (Devarim 17:15), applies only if the appointment is over Israel, as the Rambam wrote in chapter 1 of the Laws of Kings, halakha 4: "For all positions of authority in Israel, not an army commander… even one appointed over a water channel who distributes from it to the fields… that he be only from Israel." But to appoint them over their own settlements involves neither the prohibition of "lo teḥonem" nor that of authority over Israel. For these powers are included within the framework of individual civil rights, which are permitted. And perhaps we are commanded to grant the minorities in the Land local powers, just as the gentiles are commanded to establish for themselves a judicial system to judge according to the laws of their own courts, as we shall prove from the Rambam below. And this is on condition that they are loyal to the State and to the people of Israel, according to the view of the Ra'avad mentioned above.

(p) Establishing a corporation of Arab cities, villages and settlements for the purpose of central self-governing municipal rule constitutes a halakhic problem.

But to establish a national Arab council for autonomous self-rule – this is already granting incorporated national rights. For in this we recognise them as a special and separate national public. This I would be afraid to permit them even according to the method of the Ra'avad. For every corporation of cities, villages and settlements that would be conducted under one elected leadership means recognition of their national unity. But we have no clear decision on the matter.7

Perhaps the matter depends on how we interpret the carrying out of the mitzva that was said to the sons of Noaḥ, who were commanded concerning dinim, as the Rambam wrote in chapter 9 of the Laws of Kings, halakha 14, and this is his language: "And how are they commanded concerning dinim? They are obligated to seat judges and magistrates in every district to judge concerning these six mitzvot and to warn the people," etc. It is implied from these words of the Rambam that they are commanded to establish for themselves and from among themselves a system of courts and judges who will judge according to their own laws, on condition that they are careful about keeping the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ. If this halakha in the Rambam is directed at the nations of the world outside the Land, there is no proof from it for our problem. But if it is directed also at the foreigners in the Land of Israel, it implies that they are permitted to organise themselves for conducting their own internal independent life; for it is not reasonable that each city and village should maintain a magistrates' court for itself without the existence of a complete hierarchy of magistrates' courts for the whole country. And if this may be done, and we are commanded to allow the foreigners such judicial organisation, the same law applies that they are permitted to establish a union of cities and settlements for self-rule, which will include a system of courts and magistrates and an independent local police, which will be organised under a unified command of the minorities and will stand under the command of the Inspector General of the Israel Police.

However, the grave problem that stands before us in such a case of establishing a national municipal and judicial apparatus for the minorities is this: when this whole autonomous organisation is established and operates among them independently, is there not a grave danger to be expected from it, that this organisation, which will certainly be chosen in internal democratic elections, will develop into an independent government for the Arabs of the territories of Judea and Samaria and the Gaza region, which will become a source of inspiration for intrigues and struggles and dangers towards the establishment of an independent Arab state? I must admit that I see in such an organisation a seed of calamity for an Arab national and international struggle for the establishment of a Palestinian entity and an independent Arab state.

(q) There was never a Palestinian entity in the Land. Such an entity was created by the Prime Minister of Israel in the Camp David agreement.

And here I must reveal a bitter trouble that was created by us, and by the very hands of our former Prime Minister, the late Mr Menaḥem Begin, of blessed memory: he, as it were, created with his own hands the Palestinian entity. For never did any Jewish or foreign leader whatsoever dare to grant the Arabs of the Land of Israel the heritage of the Philistines who lived in the Land in the past and had a region of their own on the western shores of the Land, as it is written (Bereshit 21:34): "And Avraham sojourned in the land of the Philistines many days." And likewise later it is written (Shemot 13:17): "And God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, though it was near." The Philistines were always a stake driven in, and a root bearing gall and wormwood, for the people of Israel, and they never ceased to fight against us throughout the whole period of our existence as an independent kingdom in the Land of Israel, both in the period of the Judges and in the First Temple, until the period of the Ḥashmona'im, when the Philistines appear for the last time on the world stage, as it is written in the Book of the Ḥashmona'im; and since then their traces vanished from the world.

The Romans, in their desire to wipe out the name of Israel from the Land, changed the name of the Land of Israel after the destruction of the Second Temple to the name Palestina, after the Philistines who had dwelt in it formerly. But none of the peoples who settled in the Land after the destruction of the Second Temple identified as heirs of the Philistines, not even in name alone. The Arabs of the Land of Israel never had an independent national entity in the Land, were not called by the name Palestinians, and did not claim to inherit the rights of the Philistines in the Land. In the period of the British Mandate the Land was called by the name "Palestine – Eretz Israel", but there was no Palestinian people, and no people that lived in the Land was called by the name Philistines. And since the destruction of the Second Temple no such entity existed in the Land. And now there arose a Prime Minister of Israel, who always championed two banks to the Jordan and the wholeness of the Land, and carried out, as it were, a resurrection of the dead for the Philistine people, and created with his own hands a new national entity for the Arabs of the Land of Israel whose name is the Palestinian people. By signing a document in the Camp David agreement that the Government of Israel undertakes to provide for the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people, he caused weeping for generations. For the Arabs of Israel were never a people with national rights; they never traced themselves to the Philistines, and no such entity was known whose name is the Palestinian people. And the Arabs of the Land never constituted any national body, and were never granted any national rights whatsoever. And here it was precisely the supposedly extreme right-wing Jewish Prime Minister who created something from nothing, and with the signature of his hand gave birth to a new people in our holy Land. On a people that had perished more than two thousand years ago Mr Menaḥem Begin, of blessed memory, performed resuscitation exercises, and presented it by the name of the Palestinian people. One must fight and struggle against granting this ancient name of the Philistines to the Arabs of the Land, since there is no connection between them and the Philistines, neither biological, nor historical, nor national, nor religious. This is an arbitrary creation that has nothing of its own; rather everything was created artificially so that it could appear on the international stage as possessing historical rights in our holy Land.

(r) The Arabs of the Land of Israel have not, and never had, any national rights in the Land, but only a civil right of residence.

It is clear, therefore, from all that we have written above, that the Arabs of the Land of Israel do not have, and never had, any national entity. At most they can request personal civil rights equal to those of the other citizens of Israel, and not any national rights whatsoever.

(s) A strange question about a reality that will never occur in the Land, and therefore it is not fitting to discuss it in our house of study.

Question 3: "Following voices heard in the media, there are residents who asked: what must a Jewish settler do when Jewish soldiers, or soldiers who are not Jewish, order him, according to the command of their commanders, to leave his home, and threaten him that if he does not leave his home they will shoot him dead?"

Answer: This strange hypothetical question – I do not believe that it could ever occur in the State of Israel. For even if the soldiers receive an order at a certain stage to evacuate people in Yesha by force and at any price, it is inconceivable that the soldiers would threaten the residents to kill them by shooting if they do not leave. It is possible that the soldiers will compel them and remove them from the house by force; but to kill them intentionally, and even to threaten them with this – heaven forbid mentioning the possibility of such conduct in the State of Israel by soldiers of the Israel Defence Forces, who are the army of the Lord. Therefore I do not address this question at all.

Summary

With this I have clarified for you the view of the Torah, as far as my hand reaches, in the matters standing at the summit of our Land and our homeland that are included in your questions. And I wish to express herewith my faith and my hope, and I believe this with complete faith, that the fate and future of the Land of Israel, since we entered the era of the third redemption some hundred years ago, are determined neither by us nor by our leaders past and present, who pride themselves and boast "my power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth." It is clear to me that there is a heavenly master plan for the Land of Israel, operating without pause, for the realisation of the vision of the prophets for the future to come. This vision finds expression in six principal functions.

(t) Six messianic functions that are to be carried out in the Land.

[1] The first function is the liberation of the Land from the hands of strangers, as it is written in the Torah (Devarim 30:5): "And the Lord your God will bring you to the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it; and He will do you good and multiply you above your fathers."

And in Yeḥezkel (39:25) it is written: "Therefore thus says the Lord God: Now will I bring back the captivity of Ya'akov," and there (39:28): "And I will gather them to their own land, and I will leave none of them there any more."

[2] The second function is the ingathering of the exiles, according to the vision of the Torah (Devarim 30:3-4): "Then the Lord your God will turn your captivity and have compassion upon you, and will return and gather you from all the peoples to which the Lord your God has scattered you. If any of yours that are dispersed be at the ends of the heavens, from there will the Lord your God gather you, and from there will He take you."

[3] The third function is the establishment of independent Jewish rule in its Land, which means the establishment of government for Israel, as the Rambam writes in the Laws of Repentance (8:7), describing the days of the Messiah: "At the time when government returns to Israel." And he repeats this in the Laws of Kings (11:1): "The King Messiah is destined to arise and restore the kingdom of David to its former state, to the first government." And so the Rambam describes the days of the Messiah in the Epistle to Yemen, in the chapter that begins: "Concerning this matter, the thing will be for the days of the Messiah, may he be revealed speedily: that when the nations think that this nation will never have government and will not be redeemed from the subjugation in which they are, and all the wise men are all of one mouth in this counsel, and also the diviners with powers – the Holy One, blessed be He, will frustrate their thoughts and their false reasoning, and then the Messiah will be revealed," etc.

Thus in three places the Rambam conditions the third redemption on the establishment of government in Israel.

[4] The fourth function is the establishment of the Sanhedrin and the Great Court in Jerusalem, as the Rambam writes in the Commentary on the Mishna to tractate Sanhedrin (1:3): "And the Holy One, blessed be He, promised that they will return, as it is said (Yeshayahu 1:26): 'And I will restore your judges as at the first, and your counsellors as at the beginning; afterwards you shall be called the city of righteousness.' And this will be without doubt when the Creator, blessed be He, prepares the hearts of men, and their merit and their longing for the Name, blessed be He, and for the Torah increase, and their wisdom grows, before the coming of the Messiah." And so the Rambam writes in the Laws of Sanhedrin (14:12): "At first, when the Temple was built, the Great Court sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone… and when the order was spoiled they were exiled from place to place, and to ten places they were exiled, and finally to Tiberias, and from there the Great Court has not stood until now. And it is a tradition that in Tiberias they are destined to return first, and from there they will move to the Temple."

[5] The fifth function is repentance, as it is written in the Torah (Devarim 30:2): "And you shall return to the Lord your God and hearken to His voice… with all your heart and with all your soul." And so the Rambam writes in the Laws of Repentance (7:5): "All the prophets commanded concerning repentance, and Israel are redeemed only through repentance. And the Torah has already promised that Israel will in the end repent at the end of their exile, and immediately they are redeemed, as it is said (Devarim 30:1-3): 'And it shall come to pass, when all these things come upon you, etc., and you shall return to the Lord your God… then the Lord your God will turn,' etc."

[6] The sixth function is the building of the Temple, as Yeḥezkel prophesies (43:10-12) about the Third Temple: "You, son of man, show the house to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities, and let them measure the pattern. And if they are ashamed of all that they have done, make known to them the form of the house and its fashion, and its goings out and its comings in, and all its forms, and all its ordinances, and all its forms and all its laws, and write it in their sight, that they may keep its whole form and all its ordinances and do them. This is the law of the house: upon the top of the mountain the whole limit thereof round about…" All our Amida prayers conclude with the prayer of Ben Teima in Avot (5:25): "May it be Your will, Hashem our God and God of our fathers, that the Temple be built speedily in our days."

(u) Everything that has happened and is happening in the Land is directed by a heavenly plan imposed upon us for the realisation of the vision of the third redemption.

These are the six principal functions of the days of the Messiah. Of them we have already carried out, completely or partially, the first, second and third. And when we look carefully at what has been happening around us over the last hundreds of years, we must reach the conclusion that supreme Providence imposes the events upon us, and all of them are directed towards the realisation of the vision of the third redemption. A proof of the matter: everything that we carried out in the Land of Israel in the last hundred years, we succeeded and went from strength to strength; but everything that we did at the same time outside the Land, we failed and went from bad to worse. For the hand of the Lord was upon us in this Land, as against the removal of the Shekhina that took place at the same time outside the Land, until we reached the Holocaust and the most terrible destruction in Jewish history, when we lost six million Jews, men, women and children.

This is not the place to detail and prove the outstretched hand of the Lord upon us for good in our holy Land. But in light of the results that we have seen with our own eyes, there is a basis to believe that from Heaven they will guard us in the future too, and the inheritance of our fathers and the land of our birth, that it not be handed over into the hands of strangers. I am imbued with an inner faith that whatever is done or not done in our holy Land, from Heaven they will bring the matters round for good and for blessing, and will prevent the handing over of the sanctified territories of the Land of Israel to foreigners. All the plans of concessions and compromises directed at the sanctified Land of Israel will come to nothing, according to the vision of Yeḥezkel (28:25-26): "Thus says the Lord God: When I have gathered the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they are scattered, and shall be sanctified in them in the sight of the nations, then shall they dwell in their own land which I gave to My servant Ya'akov. And they shall dwell in it securely, and shall build houses and plant vineyards, and shall dwell securely, when I have executed judgements upon all those that despise them round about them; and they shall know that I am the Lord their God."

An addition he wrote after several months

All this was written before the disaster that the Rabin government recently brought down upon us, which made an agreement with the greatest murderer in the world in order to hand over Judea, Samaria and the Gaza Strip to the Arabs, without receiving any compensation for it. On the contrary, since the beginning of the so-called peace agreement the intifada against us has intensified, and the blood of Israel is spilled like water. This is nothing but a blindness of the senses, or a loss of the statesmanlike way of the government, which runs amok to hand over the Land of Israel into the hands of the Arabs, without their stopping for a single moment the terror and the bloodshed of the people of Israel. All our achievements in the Six-Day War are slipping out from under our hands, and in the end we shall reach the initial situation of the State of Israel. The Arabs will declare the establishment of an independent Palestinian state, and under the guise of peace with the greatest of murderers the terror against us will intensify, especially against the Jewish settlements in Yesha, until in the end war will break out between us and the Palestinian state that will arise. The situation shakes every person of sense, and we have nothing but to lean on our Father in Heaven.8

notes_en.en: In various places I changed the position of the heading, because Rav Goren wrote it as a summary and a heading, and therefore at times it is brought after the treatment of the subject; and so I placed it first so that it should be both a summary and a heading. And there is no change at all in the content in this. Likewise I noted the letters, as he noted them in the summary letter.

In the book Torat Ha-Medina, p. 119, an additional sentence is brought that is not in the responsum I received, and this is its language: "Then, in light of the fact that the government is the agent of Israel and must act only according to the consent of the public, and we can say to the government, 'I sent you to improve, not to corrupt', therefore only Jewish halakha binds us."

In the book Torat Ha-Medina, p. 120, several lines were added, apparently from the words of the editor, and this is their language: "And although in the second article that I wrote here under the name 'The Status of Government in Israel According to Halakha' we ruled that according to the Rambam we have no authority to conduct wars and to conquer the Land of Israel, nevertheless whatever we have conquered and what we have done is done for the future too. This is only if we did things for the good of the people and its will, and not when the government does acts against the will of the people and against the Torah."

See below in question 2 on these words: at first I understood that his intention was to say that these two reasons alone are the reason for the prohibition of withdrawal.
