However, Rav Goren intended that there is another additional prohibition against giving up to the Arabs, on account of "lo teḥonem", and the prohibition of "lo teḥonem" applies to them because, according to the last two reasons, they cannot be considered gerei toshav (for they do not keep the seven mitzvot, and also what they do keep they do not keep because the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded it through Moshe). However, the first reason concerns only the words of the Rambam that one does not accept a ger toshav today.

In Torat Ha-Medina, p. 123, they added: "As it is written in Midrash Tanḥuma (Lekh Lekha 19) on the verse 'Fear not, Avram' (there 15:1): And of whom was he afraid? Of Shem, whose sons he had killed – Kedorlaomer king of Elam and his three sons, as it is said: 'The sons of Shem: Elam,'" etc. And likewise they added afterwards on the verse "according to the number of the children of Israel" (Devarim 32:8) the words of Rashi: "'According to the number of the children of Israel' – for the sake of the number of the children of Israel who were destined to come forth from the sons of Shem," etc.
Torat Ha-Medina, pages 28-42, 'Holy Land and the Saving of Life from the Point of View of Halakha'.

On these words I added a question for clarification, and it is the first question in the additions to the responsum. And he clarified that here the subject is only municipal rights, but regarding autonomy he concludes that it is forbidden, because of 'lo teḥonem'.

This addition Rav Goren added many months after he sent me his responsum. And I will add further that he would always note, and mentioned too that he had heard it from Rav Aharon Kotler zt"l, that the expression "we have no one on whom to lean but our Father in Heaven" is an expression of a state of calamity and curse, as brought in the Mishna in Sota 9:15, that at the conclusion of all the calamities that came upon Israel following the destruction of the Temple and the decline of the generations, they said so. For in a normal situation we must act in order to repair, and only when we have no ability to act is there nothing left for us but to lean on our Father in Heaven.

sections.title_en: Siman 2 – Additions to the Previous Responsum
sections.body_en:
With God's help, 22 Kislev 5753

To the honourable

Rav Eliezer Melamed

Rabbi of the moshav 'Har Bracha'

and Secretary of the Rabbis of Yesha

May your peace be abundant,

In answer to your second letter (undated), in which you raise several problems concerning my first responsum of 19 Marḥeshvan 5753, concerning the halakhic status of Judea and Samaria and the Gaza region, I hereby answer you, the first first.

Answer 1

Question 1: "…Regarding what the Rav wrote on page 14 (section o), that there is a doubt as to the view of the Ra'avad in connection with autonomy: is this a doubt in practice, or perhaps, in light of what is explained at the beginning of the responsum according to the actual situation of the Arabs (who do not keep seven mitzvot and do not believe in the Torah from Sinai), even according to the Ra'avad there is a prohibition to grant them autonomy?"

What I wrote on page 14, in the first responsum, according to the method of the Ra'avad, is that in the view of the Ra'avad it is possible to grant the Arabs of Yesha private and municipal civil rights, and this too on the explicit condition that the subject is "whoever is not a member of the PLO or of another terrorist organisation and does not cooperate with them." And my words on pages 6 and 7 apply when there is a concern that they sympathise with the PLO, as I wrote there: "And even those among them who are passive and do not cooperate with the terrorists, if their heart is with those who hold that the Land of Israel does not belong to the Jews, as the Torah of Israel obligates, one must not grant them the status of ger toshav in order to receive a right of dwelling in the Land."

In addition to the above, on page 14 I did not speak at all of "autonomy", which carries within it the seed of calamity of national rights that they never had, and granting them is bound up with the Torah prohibition of "lo teḥonem". For the true prohibition of "lo teḥonem" of the Torah is when one gives gentiles national rights in the Land of Israel, which constitutes a denial of the Torah of Israel, which promises the Land of Israel to the people of Israel alone, as it is written (Bamidbar 33:52), "And you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you." And in verse 53 the Torah repeats: "And you shall dispossess the land and dwell in it, for to you I have given the land to possess it." And there in verse 55 it is said: "But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those whom you let remain of them shall be as pricks in your eyes and as thorns in your sides, and they shall harass you in the land in which you dwell."

Moreover, on that page 14 I also reject the establishment of a national Arab council for self-governing municipal rule, since this is already granting incorporated national rights. For in this we recognise them as a special and separate national public. This I am afraid to permit them even according to the method of the Ra'avad, "because every corporation of cities, villages and settlements that would be conducted under one elected leadership means recognition of their national unity." All the more so national autonomy – no one even mentions it.

Answer 2

In question 2 you asked: "On page 8 (section i) the Rav wrote that for the last two reasons it is forbidden to give up to the Arabs territories of Yesha. Is the intention that only according to these reasons… it is forbidden to give them lands of the Land of Israel, or is the intention that in addition to the mitzva of settling the Land and to the concern for life in withdrawal, and to the desecration of God's name in it, there is also added the prohibition of giving territories of the Land to one who is not a ger toshav?"

In this question there is a confusion and a misunderstanding in your words. For the three new reasons that you raise in this section, namely (a) the mitzva of settling the Land, (b) the concern for life bound up with withdrawal, and (c) desecration of God's name – I do not know what their nature is (for the matter discussed there. And see the note to section i, that in the question I thought he was speaking of settling the Land and the prohibition of withdrawal, and Rav Goren explained). For altogether, on page 8 of my first responsum, the subject is the permission for the Arabs of the Land of Israel, who have lived here privately for generations upon generations, to remain in the Land – not as a nation and not as possessors of the rights of a people in this Land; rather the subject there is the permission of their dwelling in the Land where they have lived until now, according to the method of the Rambam or according to the method of the Ra'avad alone. If so, where is there here a transgression of the mitzva of settling the Land, and what danger to life is there in the remaining of Arabs who do not sympathise with the PLO, do not cooperate with the terrorists, and admit that the Land of Israel belongs to the Jewish people? For it is of these Arabs that we spoke on page 8. Likewise, dragging desecration of God's name into your words has no meaning, for what desecration of God's name is there in our allowing the above Arabs to remain as individuals in their place of residence according to the method of the Ra'avad? The opposite is correct: harming these Arabs who are loyal to us involves desecration of God's name, as happened with the Giv'onim, with whom the children of Israel therefore made peace, because of desecration of God's name, as the Rambam wrote in chapter 6 of the Laws of Kings, halakha 5.

Answer 3

In question 3 you asked: "Is there an absolute connection between the prohibition of lo teḥonem and the law of ger toshav, so that whoever can be considered a ger toshav is not subject to the prohibition of lo teḥonem, even when the subject is extensive parts of the Land?"

The answer to this question is yes, definitely: there is a connection between the prohibition of "lo teḥonem" and the law of ger toshav. And this answer was already given by the first Chief Rabbi of the Land of Israel, the Gaon Rav Avraham Yitzḥak Ha-Kohen Kook zt"l, as we shall bring his words below, relying on the words of the Rambam in chapter 14 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations, halakha 7, who wrote: "And why is he called ger toshav? Because we are permitted to settle him among us in the Land of Israel, as we explained in the Laws of Idolatry." And more than this, the Sefer Ha-Ḥinukh wrote in mitzva 94: "The laws of the mitzva: what the Sages of blessed memory said, that if they wished to abandon idolatry, even though they had worshipped it from the outset, they are permitted to dwell in our land; and this is what is called ger toshav, that is, he is a ger with regard to dwelling in our land." So too it is implied from the Ramban, Devarim (20:6).

And this was already ruled explicitly by our master the first Chief Rabbi of the Land of Israel, the Gaon Rav Kook zt"l, in his book 'Mishpat Kohen', Laws of Shemita and Yovel, siman 63, in his letter to the Gaon our teacher Rabbi Ya'akov David of Slutzk (author of the Ridbaz commentary on the Yerushalmi), in his language there, "that Ishmaelites are called, with regard to a resting place in the land, as gerei toshav"; and he explains there afterwards that certainly one may rely on the view of the Baḥ, who objects to the Beit Yosef and infers from the language of the Tur that Ishmaelites are not like idolaters with regard to a free gift; and with regard to a resting place in the land there is a greater reasoning that they are not idolaters. And the Gaon Rav Kook concludes there: "And from the words of the Maggid Mishneh in chapter 14 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations, halakha 9, it is explicit that for a ger toshav a resting place in the land is permitted."

In addition to this, the Gaon Rav Kook zt"l raised in his book "Shabbat Ha-Aretz", chapter 12, a strange idea, that "in our time, according to the one who says that the holiness of the Land is nullified with regard to the obligations of the mitzvot dependent on the Land, the same law applies that it is nullified with regard to a resting place in the land, and it is only rabbinic," although immediately afterwards he tried to retreat from this view and wrote, "However, the view of the Rambam implies somewhat that it is not so." And he concludes there from the words of the Rambam: "And since he wrote that at a time when the Jubilee does not apply one does not accept a ger toshav with regard to the law of dwelling in the Land, it seems that he holds that although the holiness of the Land is nullified for terumot and ma'asrot and shemita and Jubilees, nevertheless for the law of the dwelling of foreigners it is not nullified. And one may say that the same law applies with regard to the prohibition of a resting place in the land."

But in the end the Gaon Rav Kook zt"l retracts this and returns to his first reasoning, and explains the words of the Rambam, who forbids settling foreigners who are not idolaters in the Land of Israel in our time because one accepts a ger toshav only at a time when the Jubilee applies, that this prohibition of the Rambam is only rabbinic. For he wrote there: "However, all this is not so compelling. For one may say that by rabbinic law in any case it is forbidden, and on this the Rambam said that at a time when the Jubilee does not apply it is forbidden to settle a ger toshav, and this is by rabbinic law; and this is also according to the method of the Rambam in the Laws of the Chosen House (6:15-16)… for he of blessed memory also holds like the reasoning of the Tosafot mentioned above, that all the mitzvot dependent on the Land have an equal law, and since the holiness of the Land is nullified, all of them are nullified." And so the Gaon Rav Kook concludes there in the end in halakha and in practice, that all the mitzvot dependent on the Land, and likewise shevi'it, and likewise the law of a resting place in the land for foreigners – all are only rabbinic. These words of the Gaon Rav Kook zt"l, which he wrote for halakha in practice, constitute a reversal from the point of view of the halakha accepted by us; and had our master Rav Kook zt"l not written them, we would not have conceived of equating the prohibition of "lo teḥonem" in the Land of Israel with the holiness of the Land regarding the mitzvot dependent on the Land.

We thus learn that in the view of our master the Gaon Rav Kook zt"l there is a double permission to give the Arabs of the Land of Israel permission of a resting place in the land: (a) because in our time the prohibition is only rabbinic, since the holiness of the Land has lapsed, and because of enmity we permit rabbinic prohibitions in many places in the Talmud [see Avoda Zara 26a: "Rav Yosef said: For a fee it is permitted, because of enmity," and see there in the Tosafot s.v. "u-remineh", and Bava Metzia 32b]; (b) in the view of the Gaon Rav Kook zt"l there is no prohibition of a resting place in the land concerning the Ishmaelites, and he uses this permission as a halakhic support for permitting the sale of the soil of the Land of Israel to foreigners in the shemita year. It emerges from the words of our master Rav Kook zt"l that in general one should not rely on the prohibition of "lo teḥonem" with regard to the Arabs of the Land of Israel.

Nevertheless, I wish to repeat and confirm the conditions that I made in my first responsum regarding the Arabs of the Land, that they are firm and established: that whoever sympathises with the PLO and does not believe that the Land of Israel was promised in its entirety to the Jews does not have the law of a ger toshav, even according to the Ra'avad, and needless to say according to the Rambam; and although he is not an idolater, it is forbidden to give him a resting place in the Land.

In addition to this, I repeat and emphasise that in my first responsum I discussed only the granting of individual permission to the Arabs of the Land of Israel to live in the Land, and not as a national body. For in spite of the words of our master the Gaon Rav Kook zt"l, it is forbidden in my humble opinion, according to the law of the Torah, to grant the Ishmaelites, who are the Arabs of the Land of Israel, and anyone who is a foreigner in the Land, sovereign rights of autonomy as an independent national body. This prohibition of granting rights of ownership over the Land of Israel is more severe than giving a resting place in the land to a private foreigner.

In addition to this, in my humble opinion our master the Gaon Rav Kook zt"l is not correct in his ruling that established that the prohibition of a resting place in the land in our time is only rabbinic. For from the Rambam it is clear that the prohibition of a resting place in the land for foreigners does not depend on the holiness of the Land with regard to the mitzvot dependent on the Land; and certainly this prohibition has no connection to the law of the majority of its inhabitants being upon it, which is a condition for the obligation of the mitzvot dependent on the Land, as the Rambam wrote in chapter 1 of the Laws of Terumot, halakha 26.

Answer 4

In question 4 you asked: "What is the status of the Arabs in the Land of Israel today? From the point of view of halakha, since they are not defined as gerei toshav, must we expel them, or perhaps, since they were already born here, we have no obligation to expel them? Etc."

I am surprised at this question of yours, since in my first responsum I established the status of the Arabs of the Land of Israel both according to the view of the Rambam and according to the view of the Ra'avad. And since according to the view of the Maggid Mishneh in the Laws of Forbidden Relations mentioned above, as in the words of the Gaon Rav Kook zt"l, even the Rambam agrees that one can give those who are not idolaters in our time permission to dwell in the Land, and certainly so is the view of the Ra'avad and his school – it follows that insofar as the subject is Arabs who are loyal to the State of Israel and admit our historical right over the Land of Israel, we are forbidden to expel them. Rather we must give them civil rights, like the citizens of Israel, without any national rights.

But if the subject is Arabs who are hostile to us and to the State of Israel, certainly we are forbidden to settle them in the Land, both according to the view of the Rambam and according to the view of the Ra'avad, since they do not keep the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ; their law is as idolaters.

In addition to this, here before you is a clear halakhic ruling of our master the Gaon Rav Kook zt"l, as above (in the answer to question 3), which establishes in halakha and in practice that the law of the Ishmaelites is as gerei toshav and they have rights of dwelling in the Land even according to the view of the Rambam,
as he wrote in his book 'Mishpat Kohen', siman 63, at the end of page 128. If so, why do you ask our opinion, when there stands before you the giant of ruling and of the spirit, in the figure of our master Rav Kook zt"l, by whose mouth we live and from whose waters we drink?

But all this is on the explicit condition that any Arab who cooperates with the terrorists, even passively, or who shows sympathy for the movements of opposition to the State of Israel, his law according to halakha is as a foreigner who transgresses daily the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ, and his law is as the law of an idolater, who loses the right of dwelling in the Land of Israel, as the Rambam rules in chapter 10 of the Laws of Idolatry, halakha 6, and as we explained thoroughly in our first responsum (section h). And the Ra'avad agrees with him in this.

As for the punishment of expulsion from the Land for members of the terror organisations, for the terrorists and their helpers, there is no doubt that from the point of view of halakha, all who participate in the intifada, whether in actual war or in throwing stones at IDF soldiers and at Jewish civilians, whether adults or minors and children, their law is to be expelled from the Land, they and their families. As our Sages of blessed memory say in tractate Sukka (56b): "The talk of the child in the market is either his father's or his mother's" (the talk of the child in the market comes from what he heard from his father or his mother). Thus the parents are found responsible for the terror actions of their children, and the punishment for this according to the law of the Torah, when our hand is strong over them, both according to the Rambam and according to the view of the Ra'avad, is expulsion from the Land, as it is written, "For I will deliver the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you" (Shemot 23:31).

This is the minimal punishment that is most effective and most halakhic, as the Rambam rules on the basis of the verse (Shemot 23:33), "They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against Me." This is said of every foreigner who transgresses the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ, and all the more so of those among the Arabs who cooperate with, or even sympathise with, the murderers and their helpers, whose law is as partners to the murder of Jews. And if they are not brought to trial, their law is expulsion from the Land, which in my humble opinion is the most effective punishment for stopping the intifada.

These are the things that I was able to answer you on your questions in your second letter, and may we merit the blessing of the Torah, "And I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down and none shall make you afraid."

Rav Shlomo Goren

A happy Festival of Lights

From the answer to question 4 in the second responsum, I published in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin no. 6, 14 Tevet 5753, Rav Goren's treatment of the expulsion of Arabs. This was after the Government of Israel had expelled four hundred terrorists and their supporters from the Land, and there was a topical interest in this responsum. The words were published in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin with the agreement of Rav Goren zt"l, and therefore, although they are repeated, they have importance, and I shall bring them exactly as they were published:

Expelling Arabs – Rav Shlomo Goren (Chief Rabbi of Israel 5733-5743)

Question: What is the status of the Arabs living today in the Land of Israel? From the point of view of halakha, must we expel them from the Land according to the law of one who is not a ger toshav, or perhaps, since they already live in the Land of Israel and were also born in it, we have no obligation to expel them? Or perhaps by the law they ought to be expelled, only because of compulsion (the state of the nation and international pressures) we cannot expel them today? (Rav Goren's answer was written on 22 Kislev 5753, and the essence of his words, with certain omissions, was published in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin no. 6 of 14 Tevet 5753.)

Answer: (a) Here before you is a clear halakhic ruling of our master the Gaon Rav Kook zt"l, which establishes in halakha and in practice that the law of the Ishmaelites is as gerei toshav and they have rights of dwelling in the Land, according to the view of the Ra'avad and even according to the view of the Rambam, as he wrote in his book 'Mishpat Kohen', siman 63. If so, why do you ask our opinion, when there stands before you the giant of ruling and of the spirit, in the figure of our master Rav Kook zt"l, by whose mouth we live and from whose waters we drink?

(b) But all this is on the explicit condition that any Arab who cooperates with the terrorists, even passively, or who shows sympathy for the movements of opposition to the State of Israel, his law according to halakha is as a foreigner who transgresses daily the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ, and his law is as the law of an idolater, who loses the right of dwelling in the Land of Israel, as the Rambam rules in chapter 10 of the Laws of Idolatry, halakha 6. As we explained thoroughly in our first responsum, all those among them who lend a hand to the intifada are suspected of the murder of Jews, whether they do so in practice, or whether they know of it and are silent and do not fight against the terrorists and murderers. The law of all of these is as those who violate the mitzva "You shall not murder", or at least the mitzva of "dinim", which are among the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ (see Rambam, Laws of Kings 9:14). And the same law applies to the Arabs of Yesha who are members of the PLO or of another terrorist organisation. Or even those among them who are passive and do not cooperate with the terrorists – and it makes no difference whether they are a majority or a minority – if their heart is with those who hold that the Land of Israel does not belong to the Jews, as the Torah of Israel obligates, one must not grant them the status of ger toshav, and they have no right of dwelling in the Land of Israel, according to the Rambam and the Ra'avad alike.

(c) In summary, there is no doubt that from the point of view of halakha, all who participate in the intifada, whether in actual war or in throwing stones at IDF soldiers and at civilians, whether adults or minors and children, their law is to be expelled from the Land, they and their families. As the Sages of blessed memory say in tractate Sukka (56b): "The talk of the child in the market is either his father's or his mother's." Thus the parents are found responsible for the terror actions of their children, and the punishment for this according to the law of the Torah, when our hand is strong over them, is expulsion from the Land, as it is said: "For I will deliver the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you" (Shemot 23:31). This is the minimal punishment that is most effective and most halakhic, as the Rambam rules on the basis of the verse (there 33), "They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against Me." This is said of every foreigner who transgresses one of the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ, and all the more so of those among the Arabs who cooperate with, or even sympathise with, the murderers and their helpers, whose law is as partners to the murder of Jews. And if they are not brought to trial, their law is expulsion from the Land, which in my humble opinion is the most effective punishment for stopping the intifada. And may we merit the blessing of the Torah: "And I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down and none shall make you afraid."

sections.title_en: Siman 4 – The Obligation to Demonstrate for Security
sections.body_en:
The security situation in the days of the Rabin government kept deteriorating; the expressions of the government's weakness spurred the terrorists to intensify their actions. In the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin no. 8, of the eve of Pesaḥ 5753, a notice of the Committee of the Rabbis of Yesha was published, with a call to protest against the government over the poor security situation. And immediately after it, a short article by Rav Goren according to this letter that he sent me. The content of these words is brought more extensively above in the first responsum, sections m-n.

The Obligation of Demonstration and Protest over the Security Situation

22 Adar 5753

To the honourable Secretariat of the Rabbis of Yesha

headed by Rav Eliezer Melamed shlit"a, rabbi of Har Bracha

May your peace be abundant for ever.

In answer to your question: what must be done after the murderous attacks that keep intensifying against us?

To our heart's grief, the helplessness of the government and the security forces has brought upon us this terrible situation, as described in Yeshayahu (37:3): "This day is a day of trouble and of rebuke and of contempt." Jewish blood is spilled like water day by day. The government's policy has made Jewish blood ownerless in our Land. Since the light of redemption shone upon us when the Lord returned the captivity of His people, we have not been in so terrible a situation; even in the period of the British Mandate our blood was not ownerless as it is today.

The police and the security forces are intended, as it were, only to protect the murderers, so that no harm befall them from the angry crowd boiling over the blood of Jews.

In light of the complete collapse of our security, it is a mitzva of the Torah to demonstrate and protest with all our strength against the government's policy, in order to fulfil the mitzva "You shall not stand by the blood of your fellow" (Vayikra 19:16), and to fulfil the vision "And the house of Ya'akov shall be a fire, and the house of Yosef a flame, and the house of Esav for stubble, and they shall kindle them and devour them" (Ovadya 1:18).

And from tractate Shabbat 55a we learn that the mitzva of rebuke and protest against the government is most severe, to the point that the transgression itself is charged to the account of the one who could have protested and did not protest. And so they said there (54b): that whoever is able to protest against the people of his city and did not protest is held responsible for the iniquity of the people of his city; and if he could have protested against the whole world and did not protest, he is held responsible for the iniquities of the whole world. And so the Rambam ruled in chapter 6 of the Laws of Character Traits, halakha 7. And in Sanhedrin 27b they expounded the verse "and they shall stumble one upon his brother": one through the iniquity of his brother; this teaches that all are guarantors for one another, for it was in their power to protest and they did not protest.

And we learned in tractate Arakhin 16b: How far does rebuke go? Rav said: until striking; and Shmuel said: until cursing; and Rabbi Yoḥanan said: until reproach. And the Rambam ruled in chapter 6 of the Laws of Character Traits, halakha 7, like the view of Rav, that a person is always obligated to rebuke the sinner until he strikes him and says to him: I will not listen. And from here we learn that the demonstrations must be sharp, but the demonstrators have no permission to use physical violence against the police and the security forces.

These demonstrations of protest must encompass all the multitudes of the house of Israel. This includes non-violent confrontation with the security forces that do not protect our lives. One must organise mighty protest gatherings of hundreds of thousands of people, everyone to whom Jewish blood is precious, to gather in the squares of the large cities with a great and bitter cry and with an unequivocal demand for the imposition of the death penalty on murderers, as it is written (Bamidbar 35:33): "And no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, but by the blood of him that shed it." This is the command of the hour placed on every Jew in this Land, to take part, with our young and with our old, in these demonstrations of protest, and in a firm demand of the government: stop immediately the bloodshed raging before our eyes, according to the command of the Torah: "If one comes to kill you, rise early to kill him."

And may we merit the fulfilment of the word of the Lord by the mouth of His prophets: "And you shall put away the evil from your midst," "and do not put innocent blood in the midst of Your people Israel."

Signing in tears,

Rav Shlomo Goren

Following the initial agreements with the PLO, the 'Oslo Accords', in which the Rabin government undertook in principle to withdraw the IDF from territories in Yesha, I sent the Rav a question. Rav Goren's answer was published in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin no. 14, on 3 Tevet 5754. Here the question and the full answer are printed.

With God's help, 11 Kislev 5754

To the honourable Rav, the Gaon Shlomo Goren shlit"a,

Chief Rabbi of Israel (5733-5743).

• To our great sorrow, a painful question has arisen recently: is a soldier who receives an order to evacuate a Jewish settlement from Yesha obligated to refuse to carry out this order because it contradicts the mitzva of settling the Land, or perhaps, since the democratically elected government has placed upon him the evacuation of a settlement, he must carry out the order?
• Recently series of educational sessions on this subject have been held in the army, and every soldier is asked: should you receive an order to evacuate a settlement, will you follow the instructions of the order or not? And since many soldiers answer that they will not carry out the order, representatives of the Education Corps explain to them that this is a democratic duty, etc., and even threaten and announce that there are severe punishments for refusing an order. And many soldiers ask whether they may hide their opinion from their commanders in order not to come into confrontation with them, something that may take revenge on them in their chances of promotion to officer rank.
• Since the subject is one of principle and general, we ask your honour to give two answers: one concise answer that we can publish widely (in tens of thousands of copies), and a second, longer answer with sources and reasons, which will be published in a narrower framework.

P.S. Incidentally to this question, I shall turn with a question that troubles many today regarding the Rav's view on the subject of the Golan. For as I understood, the Rav attributes to the Golan too the value of settling the Land, only that its level is lower; but since the Rav foresaw that the Government of Israel would not be able to withstand the international pressure and would certainly withdraw from parts of the Land, the Rav therefore permitted withdrawing from the Golan in order to preserve the essence of the sanctified Land – Judea and Samaria. For if the state of war with Syria ends, there will no longer be real pressure on Israel to give up Yesha. And the question is whether today too, after the government has agreed to enter a process whose essence is giving up Yesha, there is room to permit withdrawal from the Golan.

Eliezer Melamed

Secretary of the Rabbis of Yesha

The letter of answer:

With God's help, 15 Kislev 5754

29 November 1993

To our dear one and our friend

the great Rav, Rabbi Eliezer Melamed shlit"a

rabbi of the settlement Har Bracha and Secretary of the Rabbis of Yesha

May your peace be abundant,

To your questions of 11 Kislev 5754: whether a soldier who receives an order to evacuate a Jewish settlement from Yesha must refuse to carry out this order because it contradicts the mitzva of settling the Land, or perhaps, since the democratically elected government has placed upon him the evacuation of a settlement, he must carry out the order.

I have two answers to the above:

A. It is clear that according to halakha a soldier who receives an order that contradicts the laws of the Torah must fulfil the halakha of the Torah and not the secular order. This follows a fortiori from a king: the Sages expounded in tractate Sanhedrin 49a the verse (Yehoshua 1:18) "Whoever rebels against your command and does not hearken to your words in all that you command him shall be put to death" – could this be even regarding words of Torah? The verse teaches: "only be strong and of good courage." And Rashi explained: "'Only' – limitations; that if the king comes to nullify words of Torah, one does not listen to him." And so the Rambam ruled in the Laws of Kings (3:9): "One who nullifies the decree of the king because he was occupied with mitzvot, even a minor mitzva, is exempt; the words of the master and the words of the servant – the words of the master come first. And needless to say, if the king decreed to nullify a mitzva, one does not listen to him." All the more so one must not obey a military order that contradicts the mitzvot of the Torah. And it is clear that the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel is severe, for it is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah, as we learned in the Tosefta Avoda Zara (4:3), and as we learned in the Sifrei of the house of Rav, parashat Re'eh (piska 80), which expounds the verse "and you shall possess it and dwell in it"; they said: dwelling in the Land of Israel is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah. It is clear, therefore, that an order from the army that violates this severe mitzva has no validity. If a mitzva overrides the orders of the king, all the more so does it override the orders of the army.

From here is an answer to your doubts, where you wrote: "or perhaps, since the democratically elected government has placed upon him the evacuation of a Jewish settlement, perhaps he must carry out the order." For the king too was chosen in Israel in a democratic way[1] and by a prophet; nevertheless the king's order has no power to override the fulfilment of a mitzva, as above, even though the status of the king surpasses the status of any secular government in Israel. Certainly it is not within its authority to compel a soldier to transgress the mitzvot of the Torah.

In our case it is not only the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel that stands against the military order, but also the prohibition of "lo teḥonem", which the Sages expounded in tractate Avoda Zara 20a: do not give them (the gentiles) a resting place in the land. And so the Rambam ruled in chapter 10 of the Laws of Idolatry, halakha 4, that it is forbidden to sell land in the Land of Israel to foreigners, as the Rambam wrote there: "And why does one not sell to them? For it is said: 'lo teḥonem' – do not give them a resting place in the land; for if they have no land, their dwelling is temporary dwelling." And here the (order of) evacuation of the settlements from Judea and Samaria is in order to hand over the land of the settlements to the Arabs, which is a doubled and redoubled transgression; certainly one must not compel a soldier to transgress several severe transgressions of the Torah.

A second, additional answer to your question is that this government does not rest on a Jewish majority but on the votes of the Arabs, and from the point of view of halakha it does not have the validity of a majority. Therefore the government's instructions to evacuate the Jewish settlements have no validity or authority of the majority of the people at all. Consequently, it is clear that the soldiers must refuse orders to evacuate Jewish settlements in the Land of Israel that contradict the mitzvot of the Torah; and of this the Sages said: "The words of the master and the words of the disciple – to the words of the master one listens."

In addition to this, there is an explicit verse in the Torah (Bamidbar 33:51-55): "When you pass over the Jordan into the land of Kena'an, then you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you… and you shall dispossess the land and dwell in it, for to you I have given the land to possess it… But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those whom you let remain of them shall be as pricks in your eyes and as thorns in your sides, and they shall harass you in the land in which you dwell." All the more so we are forbidden with a most severe prohibition to evacuate Jewish settlements that were built with toil and in which Jews dwell, in order to hand them over to the Arabs, who have no portion or inheritance in this Land.

How soldiers should answer those who question them

As for question 2, how soldiers who are asked in educational sessions whether they will carry out orders to evacuate Jewish settlements should answer, my answer is that they must be silent and not answer these questions. For they are forbidden to lie and say that they will obey the order, for "keep far from a false matter"; and they also need not answer that they will violate the order, so as not to arouse hatred against them. Therefore it is better that they be silent and not answer it at all, and fulfil the saying of the Sages: "A word is worth a sela, silence two sela'im."[2]

This is my clear answer on the matter, and you are permitted to summarise it as necessary. I could not shorten it and answer you without the above reasons.

With the blessing of the Torah and the Land,

Rav Shlomo Goren

P.S. As for what you ask in the margin of the letter about my view now regarding the Golan[3] – for the answer to this question I need lengthy words, and therefore I shall refrain from answering it now; and there is yet a vision for the problem of the Golan.[4]

S.G.

From the words of the Ratziya Kook zt"l (section 3 of a proclamation written on 14 Elul 5727, brought in Eretz Ha-Tzvi p. 19): "There is no aspect of permission whatsoever for this Torah prohibition of handing over our lands to gentiles, God forbid, permanently and absolutely. And therefore the obligation is placed on every person of Israel, and on every great Torah scholar of Israel, and on every soldier in Israel, to prevent and hold this back with all courage and strength, and from Heaven they will help us."

notes_en.en: I asked him afterwards about the source for this, and he answered that one can rely on the Gemara in Berakhot 55a: "Rabbi Yitzḥak said: One does not appoint a leader over the community unless one consults the community." And I added this in what was published in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin.

I must relate here that at first Rav Goren wanted to answer that the soldiers are obligated to say that they will not fulfil the order, and so too he expressed himself orally in the media. And in a talk in the yeshiva he brought a proof for this (perhaps from the Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma ch. 4, §9: "… that it is forbidden to alter words of Torah even though there is danger, and one is obligated to give one's life for it"). And I argued that if they say nothing, what prohibition will they transgress? And I went on to urge him to be lenient in this for the officers or soldiers who wish to advance in the army, and with difficulty he consented to agree that they are not obligated to say the truth, provided that they do not say that they will obey the order; and so he wrote in his answer. However, it is clear that a soldier who would say courageously that he would refuse would merit great honour from Rav Goren.
My question was based on things he had said to me orally.
And in the end we did not merit that he explain these words at length.

sections.title_en: Siman 6 – Words of Encouragement to the Settlers
sections.body_en:
From Rav Shlomo Goren
These words were published at the foot of the responsum on 'Refusing an Order' in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin 14, 3 Tevet 5754.

25 Kislev 5754

To Rav Eliezer Melamed, peace.

In accordance with your request, I hereby pass on to you words of encouragement to the settlers, as a conclusion to my answer on refusing the instructions of the government and the army to evacuate settlements.

And in these days of storm and tempest, when the blood of Israel is spilled like water and the Government of Israel is about to destroy all that was achieved with the blood of our sons, and we see the fall, at the hands of murderers, of heroes of strength and spirit from among the settlers, as they defend with their bodies and their spirit the wholeness of our holy Land – in these days the whole people is obligated to hold up in praise its sons and builders, the settlers in Judea, Samaria and the Katif region, sanctifiers of the Name of Heaven, who stand day by day on the line of fire, giving their lives and risking their lives for the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel, in its plain meaning.

Let your spirit not fall because of the terrible national and security situation that has deteriorated through the government that rests on an Arab majority, all of whose decisions are directed at concessions of the inheritance of our fathers. Do not despair of the hope of preserving the wholeness of our Land. The heroic and historic struggle for the inheritance of the fathers must continue. We must mobilise the whole people in the Land and in the Diaspora to your help. We shall all stand as a fortified wall against the betrayers of our Land and of our holy Torah. We shall say to the so-called government of "peace" the vision of Yeshayahu (59:8): "The way of peace they know not, and there is no justice in their paths… whoever treads in it does not know peace." And "There is no peace, says my God, for the wicked" (Yeshayahu 57:21); "Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand; for God is with us" (Yeshayahu 8:10). The promise of the Holy One, blessed be He, in the Covenant between the Pieces (Bereshit 15:18), "To your seed I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river," will stand for ever and to all eternity.

sections.title_en: Siman 7 – The Status of a Government Not Supported by a Jewish Majority
sections.body_en:
In the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin no. 16, 30 Shevat 5754, the responsum of Rav Goren zt"l was published under the heading: "The Rabin Minority Government Has No Authority Today and Its Instructions Have No Binding Force", by the Gaon Rav Shlomo Goren (Chief Rabbi of Israel 5733-5744).

It should be noted that this responsum was written a short time after a demand was raised to put him on trial; yet although the things he wrote could arouse opposition on the part of political, legal and media bodies, Rav Goren zt"l did not shrink back and continued to say his word boldly. I remember that in that period, when he came to his weekly shiur in Har Bracha, students asked him out of concern whether there was not a fear that they would harm him, as was being said in the media. But he answered dismissively: "What are you afraid of? I am not afraid!" and continued his shiur as was his custom. Moreover, after they would attack him, he would answer those who reviled him. And once, after a whole day in which he responded in all the media, in Hebrew and in English, on the matter of our ownership of the Land of Israel and 'refusing an order', he said to me in the evening roughly this: "This was a most important day; thank God, all day I spoke in various media, on the radio, on television (they came to his home and to the Idra yeshiva to interview him) and to the press, and let us hope that with God's help the words will act for good."[1]

After the publication of the words on "the status of a government not supported by a Jewish majority" too, they interviewed him on the radio, and he explained his words forcefully. And in order to stir up dissension and make his position seem strange among the listeners, they asked him whether Druze voters and Knesset members can be counted towards the majority. And he was greatly pained by this question, which was asked on a live broadcast, for he loved the Druze community, whose sons serve in the army; but he did not agree to change from the truth, and stood by his view, the view of the Torah, that the votes of Druze too cannot decide on these subjects. His words published in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin were taken from the responsum he wrote to me, with changes of wording [as I understood, while he relied on me, and he did not even demand to see the changes before they were sent to print; but I asked him many times by telephone, for the sake of clarifying the words]. Here his full responsum is brought:

With God's help, 23 Tevet 5754

To the honourable our master the Rav, the Gaon Shlomo Goren shlit"a

Great peace,

In his answer to us on the question whether a soldier must refuse an order when it contradicts halakha, the Rav also wrote: "This government does not rest on a Jewish majority but on the votes of the Arabs, and from the point of view of halakha it does not have the validity of a majority; therefore the government's instructions to evacuate the Jewish settlements have no validity or authority of the majority of the people at all."

• What are the halakhic foundations of this determination?
• Does this rule apply to all the instructions of a government that has no Jewish majority, or perhaps only to its instructions on matters of principle, and what are the matters of principle?

Further questions which perhaps there is no need to answer already now are:

• In defining a Jewish majority, is the subject a majority of Jewish Knesset members, or is the subject the position of the majority of Jewish voters? That is, the Arab Knesset members do not represent the full strength of the Arab vote. For example, with the Shas party the government has a majority of Jewish Knesset members, but apparently there is no majority of Jewish voters, since more than fifteen Knesset members of the left were elected by Arab votes, and the votes of about two Knesset members were disqualified because their parties did not pass the threshold.
• Do critical decisions require, according to halakha, a qualified majority? Can one perhaps learn from capital cases, in which to convict one needs a majority of thirteen judges against ten, that there is a need for a qualified majority?

With thanks in advance,

Eliezer Melamed

Secretary of the Rabbis of Yesha, in the name of the Rabbis of Yesha

The letter of answer:

With God's help, 26 Tevet 5754

9 January 1994

To my dear one, guardian of the charge of the Torah and of our holy Land,

Rav Eliezer Melamed shlit"a

Secretary of the Rabbis of Yesha, rabbi of the moshav Har Bracha

May your peace be abundant for ever,

To your question in your letter of 23 Tevet 5754 on my answer to you of 3 Tevet 5754, in connection with the status and authority of the Government of Israel today, when this government has no Jewish majority in the Knesset but rests on the votes of Arabs. And I wrote to you that from the point of view of halakha this government does not have the validity of a majority; therefore its instructions, if they are issued, to evacuate settlements in Yesha, have no validity or authority of the majority of the people. And you now ask:

(a) What are the halakhic foundations of this determination?

(b) Does this rule apply to all the instructions of a government that has no Jewish majority, or perhaps only to its instructions on matters of principle, and what are the matters of principle?

Answer: My halakhic ruling, in everything concerning the authority of the government and its legal-halakhic status when (the government) does not rest on a Jewish majority but on Arab Knesset members who complete the majority on which this government rests – among whom are Arab Knesset members who hate Zion, who are ready to lend a hand to the destruction of the State and deny our national and historical right over the Land of Israel – is that its decisions have no authority or validity. And this is because there is not a shadow of doubt that these Arab Knesset members are not to be counted towards the majority of the government.

This we learn from many halakhic sources.

The first source, that the Arabs in the Land of Israel have no right to constitute part of the government and to complete the majority of the government, can be learned from the words of the Rambam, who wrote in the Laws of Kings (1:4) on the verse in Devarim (17:15), "You may not set a foreigner over you, who is not your brother": "And not for kingship alone, but for all positions of authority in Israel: not an army commander, not an officer of fifty or an officer of ten, even one appointed over a water channel who distributes from it to the fields; and needless to say a judge or a nasi – that he be only from Israel, as it is said: 'from among your brothers you shall set a king over you' – all appointments that you make shall be only from among your brothers." And so we learned in tractate Kiddushin (76b): "They came before Rav Yosef; he said to them: We learned: 'You shall surely set a king over you… from among your brothers' – all appointments that you make shall be only from among your brothers."

And in the Sefer Ha-Ḥinukh (mitzva 498) he wrote: "Among the laws of the mitzva is what the Sages of blessed memory said, that one appoints as head of any authority only from the seed of Israel, even one appointed over a water channel who distributes from it to the fields. And this prohibition applies regarding kingship at a time when Israel are on their land in their settlement, and it is among the warnings that are on the whole public; and regarding other positions of authority in Israel this prohibition applies in every place that they are, that they are forbidden by the Torah to appoint over the public a person who is not of the children of Israel." So far.

We thus learn from these words that Arab Knesset members do not have the status of Knesset members in everything concerning the authority of their jurisdiction over Jews. But their authority of jurisdiction extends solely over the Arabs, as we find in the Rambam, Laws of Kings (9:14): "And how are they (the gentiles) commanded concerning dinim? They are obligated to seat judges and magistrates (gentiles) in every district to judge concerning these six mitzvot, and to warn the people." It follows from this that the restrictions on appointments of gentiles to any positions of authority are only on being appointed over Jews; but wherever the authority is over gentiles, they may, and perhaps they are commanded to, be appointed to all the positions of authority directed at gentiles. But wherever the appointment is directed at Jews, one must not appoint them to anything involving authority, as the Torah warns (Devarim 17:15): "From among your brothers you shall set a king over you" – "all appointments that you make shall be only from among your brothers", as the author of the Sefer Ha-Ḥinukh emphasises that they are forbidden by the Torah to appoint over the public a person who is not of the children of Israel.

However, notwithstanding this Torah prohibition against granting powers of government to gentiles over Jews, the question arises whether this Torah prohibition invalidates the appointment even after the fact; so that if they appointed gentiles to authority over Israel in violation of the prohibition, and transgressed the warning of the Torah that forbade appointing over the public a person who is not of the children of Israel – whether after the fact the appointment takes effect and he possesses authority by this appointment, also over Israel, or perhaps even after the fact the appointment has no legal validity because it is against the mitzvot of the Torah. It is reasonable to assume that this halakhic problem depends on the dispute of Abaye and Rava in tractate Temura (4b): Abaye says: anything about which the Merciful One said "do not do", if one did it, it is effective; for if you think it is not effective, why is he lashed? And Rava said: it has no effect at all, and the reason he is lashed is because he transgressed the word of the Torah. And wherever Abaye and Rava disagree, the halakha is like Rava, except in the six cases known by the acronym ya'al kegam, as we find in tractate Bava Metzia (22b). It follows that even after the fact, if they chose gentiles and granted them powers of government and chose them as Knesset members, no authority is granted to them over the Jewish public, and consequently they are not counted towards the majority to decide on national matters of the Government of Israel.

This decision, whether after the fact, when they appointed gentiles to rule over Israel, the appointment has legal validity or not, depends also on a further problem of principle, namely: wherever it is written in the Torah "you may not" (lo tukhal), does it mean that he is not permitted only in the first instance, or that even after the fact what they did does not take effect? As we find in the Sifrei of the house of Rav on parashat Ki Tetze (Devarim 21:16), on the verse "he may not make the son of the beloved the firstborn before the son of the hated, who is the firstborn," they expounded in the Sifrei, piska 216: "'He may not make firstborn' – this teaches that he is not permitted to make firstborn. Could it be that he is not permitted to make firstborn, but if he did make firstborn he is made firstborn? The verse teaches: 'he may not make firstborn' – thus if he made firstborn, he is not made firstborn." It may be that the same law applies in our case, where it is written "you may not set a foreigner over you": if he set a foreigner over him, it is as though he did not set him. However, the above verse "he may not make firstborn" is also subject to a great dispute between the Sifrei and the Yerushalmi in tractate Bava Batra, chapter 8, halakha 4, and between Rabbi Ḥaggai and Rabbi Elazar in the Yerushalmi there. For we learned there in the Yerushalmi: Rabbi made the firstborn equal to his brother. Rabbi Ḥaggai said to them: Is there not a verse, "he may not make firstborn"? Rabbi La'zar said: By the Temple service, he can, but he is not permitted. Here before us is the method of Rabbi Elazar, who disagrees with the Sifrei and holds that the prohibition "he may not make firstborn" means in the first instance, but after the fact he can transfer the birthright from his firstborn son.

So too we find in the Sifrei on parashat Re'eh (Devarim 12:17, piska 72): "'You may not eat within your gates' – Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa says: I can, but I am not permitted. Similarly you say (Yehoshua 15:63): 'And the Yevusi, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Yehuda could not drive them out' – they could, but they were not permitted." And Rashi explained there: because Avraham had made a covenant with them when he took from them the Cave of Makhpela, etc. But from there we have no proof whether, wherever it is written "may not", if they transgressed the prohibition what they did is done. However, the Ramban, in parashat Ki Tetze on the verse "he may not make firstborn", writes: one who makes the firstborn equal to his brother in his inheritance transgresses a negative and a positive commandment, and even so his words do not stand in law. The same law applies regarding our problem concerning the prohibition "you may not set a foreigner over you", which the Ramban equates with the prohibition "he may not make firstborn": after the fact, if they appointed a foreigner over Israel, the appointment does not take effect in the view of the Ramban.[2]

A further halakhic reason not to count Arabs towards the government's majority

There is yet another halakhic reason not to count Arabs towards the government's majority, on the basis of the Gemara in tractate Sanhedrin (26a), which expounds the verse in Yeshayahu (8:12), "Do not say 'conspiracy' of all that this people says 'conspiracy'." And the Sages expounded: that is, it is a conspiracy of the wicked, and a conspiracy of the wicked is not counted. And the intention of the verse, according to what is said there in the Gemara: when Sanḥeriv was besieging Jerusalem, Shevna, who was over the house, and the majority of the public in Jerusalem, wished to surrender to Sanḥeriv and hand Jerusalem over to him; but King Ḥizkiyahu and the minority of the people who were with him opposed surrender to Sanḥeriv. And Shevna, who was appointed over Ḥizkiyahu's house, wrote a note and sent it to Sanḥeriv outside Jerusalem by an arrow, saying: Shevna and his faction have made peace to serve you; Ḥizkiyahu and his faction have not made peace, as it is said (Tehillim 11:2): "For lo, the wicked bend the bow, they have made ready their arrow upon the string." And King Ḥizkiyahu was afraid lest, heaven forbid, the Holy One, blessed be He, would incline His mind with the majority who wished to make peace with Sanḥeriv. A prophet came and said to Ḥizkiyahu: "Do not say 'conspiracy' of all that this people says 'conspiracy'," that is, it is a conspiracy of the wicked, and a conspiracy of the wicked is not counted. And Rashi explained there: "Do not say 'conspiracy'" – do not think in your mind that the count of Shevna will be considered a count to be considered a majority, because it is a conspiracy of the wicked and is not counted.

We thus learn that although Shevna had a majority of public opinion in Jerusalem to make peace with Sanḥeriv and not fight him, and Ḥizkiyahu had only a minority of the people, the prophet ruled that the majority of the wicked who sought to surrender to Sanḥeriv is not considered a majority as against the minority that was loyal to the king, who did not agree to surrender to Sanḥeriv. The same law applies to our problem: the majority that rests on Arabs, among them those known for their hatred of Israel – one must not count them towards the majority, and one must not count them and the leftist Knesset members who seek to surrender to the terrorists in order to complete the majority in the Knesset.[3] These Arabs certainly must not be counted as a majority in order to hand over parts of the Land of Israel to the Arabs. For their law is as the majority of Shevna, who sought to surrender to Sanḥeriv and hand Jerusalem over to him. From this it is clear that the Arabs among the Knesset members who support the government in order to hand over the sanctified half of the Land of Israel to the murderers are a conspiracy of the wicked and are not counted, and the present government is found to act only by virtue of a minority of the people, and loses its authority.

This halakhic ruling applies to all the government's instructions that do not have the support of a Jewish majority.

As for your second question, whether this halakhic ruling applies to all the instructions of the government that has no Jewish majority (or perhaps only to its instructions on matters of principle, and what are the matters of principle): my answer is that on every subject on which the government does not have the support of a Jewish majority in the Knesset, its decisions are neither firm nor established, since they are based on a minority of the Jewish people; and it is a great rule in the Torah in every matter of law and judgement, "to incline after the majority" (Shemot 23:2). Therefore a government that rests on Arabs who complete its majority is considered a minority government in every respect.

The one who signs with the blessing of the Torah,

Rav Shlomo Goren

* *

The words of my teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook zt"l

on a minority government

Following the elections after the Yom Kippur War, two governments of a Jewish minority arose. The first by Golda Meir, a government that survived only a month. The second by Yitzḥak Rabin (who already then sinned in this). The Ratziya went out with vigorous protests against the government and against the National Religious Party, which agreed to join it. He demanded that first they dismantle the minority government completely, and only afterwards could the NRP join. The NRP joined both governments (see Ba-Ma'arakha Ha-Tziburit p. 109). The quotation below is section 2 of a proclamation written on 17 Tammuz 5734, brought in "Eretz Ha-Tzvi" p. 69 (and see there a whole chapter on this subject):

"Sanctification of the Name is the foundation and root of the whole Torah, and desecration of the Name is the foundation and root of the destruction of the whole Torah. Sanctification of the Name is the honour of the Name, and it is revealed in the honour of the people of the Name, His near one and His treasure – 'And I will dwell in the midst of My people' – 'and it shall be sanctified by My glory', in the exaltation of its horn, its salvation and its redemption, in the glory of its sovereignty and its state. A desecration of the Lord, like none other, of the Name of God, blessed be He, Creator of the world, who calls its generations and sets its borders, the borders of His peoples and of His people, His portion, is the tragicomedy of the disgrace of our people and our state in assembling this minority government over our state. And 'one does not give credit in desecration of the Name.' For rot there is no repair, no healing and no improvement in joining it, heaven forbid, but only in its fundamental and absolute disqualification and annulment – and in a fundamental and radical renewal of health."

notes_en.en: Incidentally, in a survey published in those days in 'Yedi'ot Aḥaronot', carried out by the 'Daḥaf' institute under the direction of Dr Mina Tzemaḥ, it was found that 54% rejected taking measures against Rav Goren, as against 41% who supported taking measures against him. Likewise 32% supported refusing orders to evacuate settlements. Apparently the courageous and clear words of Rav Goren did indeed influence public opinion in their time.

In the bulletin I shortened this because of the difficulty and length of the words, and in place of the three paragraphs "However", "This decision", "So too", I wrote: "And if they transgressed and appointed them, this appointment has no validity or authority, as emerges from the view of Rava in Temura (4b). And so in the Sifrei (Devarim 21:16), piska 216. And the Ramban in parashat Ki Tetze on the verse 'he may not make firstborn'."
In the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin I omitted the sentence about the leftist Knesset members.
