With God's help, 8 Tevet 5754

20 January 1994

To my dear one,

guardian of the holy charge in our holy Land and its convocations,

Rav Eliezer Melamed shlit"a

Secretary of the Rabbis of Yesha

and rabbi of the moshav Har Bracha

May your peace be abundant for ever,

In your letter to me of 19 Tevet you ask:

• Are soldiers permitted to refuse to carry out an order that is at root political, such as dispersing demonstrations and blocking settlement, and to claim that this is the task of the police and not of the people's army?
• If according to halakha they are obligated to carry out the order although it contradicts the correct policy according to the Torah, must they carry it out as though compelled by a demon, and thereby minimise their participation in this action?
• Must soldiers protest against these orders, and how should they protest?

Answer

In order to answer your first question, we must establish the view of halakha regarding the demonstrations held against the government's policy of handing over parts of the sanctified Land of Israel to the Arabs and to the greatest of murderers. For the covenant that the government made with the head of the PLO terror organisation in the world flagrantly contradicts the Torah of Moshe our teacher, since the Torah warns us (Devarim 7:2): "You shall make no covenant with them, nor show them favour (lo teḥonem)," and likewise it is written (Bamidbar 33:51-52): "When you pass over the Jordan into the land of Kena'an, then you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you," "and you shall dispossess the land and dwell in it, for to you I have given the land to possess it," "But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those whom you let remain of them shall be as pricks in your eyes and as thorns in your sides, and they shall harass you in the land in which you dwell." Likewise there are many warnings in the Torah not to hand over parts of the Land of Israel to foreigners, such as the verse (Shemot 23:33): "They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against Me." And this government, in the covenant it made with the head of the organisations of murderers, violated all the mitzvot of the Torah on this matter. Therefore it is clear that on every Jew who keeps Torah and mitzvot there is placed an obligation to protest and demonstrate against these severe violations of the Torah of Israel by the Government of Israel.

The mitzva of protest against a destructive policy of the government is a mitzva of the Torah, as it is written (Vayikra 19:17): "You shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him." And the Rambam already ruled in chapter 6 of the Laws of Character Traits, halakha 7: "Whoever is able to protest and does not protest is held responsible for the iniquity of these, since he was able to protest against them." And so we learned in tractate Shabbat 54b: "Whoever is able to protest against the people of his city is held responsible for the people of his city, and whoever is able to protest against the whole world is held responsible for the whole world."

This mitzva of protest of the Torah can be fulfilled through demonstrations held by individuals and by the multitude of the people, as a protest against the violation of the Torah by the Government of Israel, on condition that the demonstrations are held without violence, as we learned from tractate Arakhin 16b, where they asked how far the mitzva of rebuke goes. And Rav and Shmuel disagreed on this question. Rav said: until striking, that is, until the person being rebuked becomes angry and strikes the one rebuking; and Shmuel said: until cursing, that is, until he curses the one rebuking, as Rashi explained there. But the one rebuking is forbidden to act with violence against the sinner. The same law applies in everything concerning the security forces: it is forbidden to act against them with physical violence.

We thus learn that soldiers sent to disperse demonstrations are agents for a transgression, since they are sent to act against the laws of the Torah. And we have already clarified in our responsum of principle of 15 Kislev 5754 (29/11/93) that a soldier who receives an order to violate the laws of the Torah must refuse to fulfil such an order, as the Rambam rules in chapter 3 of the Laws of Kings, halakha 9: "One who nullifies the decree of the king because he was occupied with mitzvot, even a minor mitzva, is exempt; the words of the master and the words of the disciple – the words of the master come first. And needless to say, if the king decreed to nullify a mitzva, one does not listen to him."

Therefore it must be clearly established that every demonstration whose aim is to protest against the destructive policy of the government of handing over the holiest parts of the Land of Israel into the hands of the greatest of murderers of the terror organisations in the world – that policy is in complete contradiction to the Torah of Moshe our teacher, and the demonstration against the agreement is a positive commandment of the Torah according to the verse "You shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him." Therefore the soldiers who are called to disperse by force these non-violent demonstrations of those faithful to the Torah must refuse to fulfil this order.

Also, the supreme purpose of the IDF is not to act against Jews and to prevent them from fulfilling the mitzvot of the Torah, but to defend the people of Israel against every enemy and foe from outside, and not to clash with Jews who come to fulfil the mitzvot of the Torah.

This is my clear answer according to halakha in everything concerning an order that soldiers of Israel receive to disperse by force quiet demonstrations against the covenant that the Government of Israel made with the greatest of murderers.

According to this answer there is no room for the second question in your letter.

The one who writes and signs in honour of the Torah and our holy Land,

Rav Shlomo Goren

After the events at the Cave of Makhpela, in which dozens of Muslims were killed by Dr Baruch Goldstein, an initiative was raised in the government to destroy the Jewish settlement in Hebron. Following this I sent a question to Rav Goren. It should be noted that Rav Goren zt"l felt an especially deep connection to Hebron. In the Six-Day War, when the forces began to move in the direction of Hebron, Rav Goren urged his driver to travel to Hebron, and it turned out that they arrived first at the Cave of Makhpela and captured it, and no one stood before them, for the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them. His answer was published in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin no. 17, 6 Nisan 5754.[1]

With God's help, 23 Adar 5754

6 March 1994

To the honourable Secretary of the Rabbis of Yesha

Rav Eliezer Melamed shlit"a

and rabbi of the settlement Har Bracha

May your peace be abundant,

In your letter of 19 Adar 5754 you write as follows: "Following the threats of government ministers to destroy the Jewish settlement in Hebron, I ask what is the attitude of halakha to these threats, and how must one respond to these threats?"

Answer: The threats of the government ministers (in the Jewish-minority government) against the Jewish settlement in the holy city of Hebron, may it be built and established speedily in our days, amen, shake and outrage to the depths of the soul every Jew loyal to his people and his Land. For the Jewish settlement in Hebron is the oldest historical settlement in the Land of Israel. Hebron is the city of the Patriarchs and the cradle of the kingdom of the house of David, in which (a Jewish settlement) existed since the destruction of the Second Temple, and was destroyed in the month of Av of the year 5689, 1929, in the terrible pogrom that the murderous Arabs of Hebron carried out in the holy Hebron yeshiva, which had been transferred in its entirety from Slobodka in Lithuania. They did this under the guidance of the qadis of Hebron, who instructed them to murder and rape the Jewish women of the residents of Hebron, and they did so; and in total they murdered 64 Jews of the yeshiva and of the residents of the city on the holy Shabbat day and raped many women, before the eyes of the sun and the moon, according to the instructions of the muezzins in the mosques. And from this terrible pogrom there remained as survivors a few Jews who succeeded in hiding until the wrath passed.

The abysmal hatred of the Arabs of Hebron for the Jews and their acts of murder against Jews can be learned also from another terrible historical crime that the Arabs of Hebron committed in the War of Independence, in the month of Iyar 5708, in the year 1948. After the Etzion Bloc, with its four points, surrendered to the Arab Legion, signed a deed of surrender, handed over their weapons to the Legion and raised white flags, an armed Arab mob came from Hebron and killed all who remained alive: 164 fighters who remained in the Bloc were killed after the surrender, and not a soul of them remained, except for one signaller who was wounded and was taken out of the Bloc while still alive.

The Arab rioters also did not bury the murdered, but left them in the communication trenches as food for the birds of the heavens and the beasts of the earth, and in the bunkers that they destroyed with explosives. A year after the killing I received authorisation from the armistice commission to enter the Bloc in order to gather the bones of the fallen. The Arab mob murdered and plundered everything that was in the Bloc and left scorched earth in the Bloc. This is a most terrible example of the murderous fury that always beat among the Arabs of Hebron, the worst of all the murderers who operated in the Land.

And since the pogrom that the Arabs of Hebron carried out against the Jews in the year 5689, 1929, the Jewish settlement in Hebron was destroyed, and they did not return to it until the liberation of the city in the Six-Day War.

Hebron was the beginning of the kingdom of David, who reigned in Hebron seven years; and Reḥav'am son of King Shlomo built Hebron as a fortified city (as it is written in II Divrei Ha-Yamim 11:6). And when the children of the exile came up from Babylon, at the beginning of the Second Temple, they settled in Hebron and its towns, as it is written in the book of Neḥemya (11:25). And apparently Hebron remained a fortified city in the hands of the Edomites, who conquered it from the Jews, until the period of the Ḥashmona'im. Then Yehuda the Maccabee and his brothers captured Hebron and its towns, "and they pulled down the stronghold and burned the towers round about with fire" (I Maccabees 5:65).

The great traveller Rabbi Binyamin of Tudela visited Hebron in the year 1171 and found it ruined, with only one Jew living in it: "And in the valley of the field, in the field of Makhpela, there is the city, and it was a synagogue of the Jews in the days of the Ishmaelites; but if a Jew comes who gives a fee to the gatekeeper of the cave, he opens for him an iron door that was made in the days of our fathers, peace be upon them, and a person goes down below with a lit candle in his hand, etc.; and there are barrels full of bones of Israel, for the house of Israel used to bring their dead there, each one the bones of his fathers, and lay them there to this day. And at the edge of the field of Makhpela is the house of Avraham our father, peace be upon him, and a spring before the house, and they do not allow a house to be made there, out of respect for Avraham." Also at the time that Salah al-Din conquered Hebron the Jewish settlement in Hebron did not cease, until it was destroyed in the Arab pogrom in the year 5689, 1929.

In the year 1211 Rabbi Shmuel son of Rabbi Shimshon and his companions found Jews in it who went at midnight to the Cave of Makhpela to pray. In the year 1267 the Ramban came to Hebron, and according to the words of R. Y. Ḥelo of the 14th century there was then in Hebron a large community of Jews, and many of them were weavers and engaged in dyeing wool and in glass-blowing, which to this day is one of the great branches of commerce in Hebron.

In the 15th century, in the year 1490, about 20 Jewish families lived in Hebron, among them anusim of Spain who had fled from the Inquisition to Hebron. And in the 16th century there were only 10 families in Hebron; and Rabbi Malkiel Ashkenazi bought in the year 1540 from the Karaites a large courtyard and founded a Jewish community there, and from then on the number of Jews in Hebron increased.

In the year 1619 a plague broke out in Hebron, and many of its Jewish residents fled to Gaza, among them the Gaon author of 'Ḥesed Le-Avraham'. And when the plague was halted the Jews returned to it.

In the year 1813 the rabbis of Hebron were arrested by the authorities in order to force the community to pay a tax that had been imposed on it, and the rabbis of the city sent emissaries to Europe to send money to redeem the prisoners; in Amsterdam a special committee was founded to help them. And in the summer of the year 1834 Ibrahim Pasha conquered Hebron, and his army carried out a pogrom against the Jews, but the Jewish settlement remained there.

In the year 1850 Ḥabad Ḥasidim, who lived in Safed and Tiberias, came up to Hebron and founded a special community in Hebron. And from then on the people of Ḥabad constituted the majority of the Ashkenazi Jews in the city.

In the year 1910 (5670) the number of Jews in Hebron rose to one thousand one hundred. Among the holy places in Hebron, apart from the Cave of Makhpela, is the ancient synagogue named after Avraham our father, in which they pray on Shabbat and festivals. Until the Jewish destruction of Hebron in 5689 there were in Hebron four synagogues – two of Sephardim and two of Ashkenazim – and four houses of study and yeshivot.

From all this we see that the Jewish community existed in Hebron almost continuously for thousands of years, from the period of the Ḥashmona'im onwards. It is important to mention that also in the period of the Second Temple the eyes of the kohanim in the Temple were turned towards Hebron at the time of the slaughter of the morning tamid offering, as we learned in tractate Yoma (3:1): "The appointed one said to them: Go out and see whether the time of slaughter has arrived. If it had arrived, the one who sees says: Barkai (the dawn has flashed). Matitya ben Shmuel says: Has the whole face of the east become light, as far as Hebron? And he says: Yes." The Jerusalem Talmud explains why he mentions Hebron: because he comes to recall the merit of the Patriarchs buried in Hebron.

At the beginning of the first conquest of the Land by Yehoshua bin Nun, Hebron was sanctified as a city of refuge, as it is written in Yehoshua (20:7): "And they set apart Kedesh in the Galil in the hill country of Naftali, and Shekhem in the hill country of Efrayim, and Kiryat Arba, which is Hebron, in the hill country of Yehuda."

We thus learn from all that has been said that Hebron is the second holy city in importance in the Land, after Jerusalem. And the Jewish settlement was not uprooted from it except in the pogrom of the Arab rioters in Hebron in the year 5689. And at the time of the renewal of the Jewish settlement in Hebron in the Six-Day War, the people blessed "Blessed is He who sets the border of the widow." This is the blessing established in halakha at the time when a Jewish settlement that was destroyed in the Land of Israel is re-established, as we learned in tractate Berakhot (58b): "One who sees the houses of Israel in their settled state says: Blessed is He who sets the border of the widow."

From all this it is clear that the destruction of the Jewish settlement in Hebron now is a religious-historical-national crime that cannot be atoned for, and it would require tearing as over a dead person, according to the explicit halakha in the Talmud in tractate Mo'ed Katan (26a): "One who sees the cities of Yehuda in their destruction says: 'Your holy cities have become a wilderness' (Yeshayahu 64), and tears." And so the Rambam rules in chapter 5 of the Laws of Fasts, halakha 16, and the Shulḥan Arukh Oraḥ Ḥayim siman 561, se'if 1. And tearing over the destruction of a city in Yehuda has the law of tearing over one's father and mother who died, as we learned in tractate Mo'ed Katan there: "And these are tears that are not mended: one who tears over his father and over his mother, and over the cities of Yehuda, and over the Temple, and over Jerusalem that were destroyed." It is implied from this that from the point of view of halakha the renewed destruction of Hebron has the law of putting to death the fathers of the nation; that is, one must judge the destruction of Hebron, heaven forbid, according to the law of the saving of people's lives, to which the halakha of "let him be killed and not transgress" applies. So one must judge the destruction of the Jewish settlement in Hebron as the murder of people's lives, over which one must tear a tear, as over a dead person.[2]

According to halakha – the destruction of the Jewish settlement of Hebron by the hands of Jews has the law of "let him be killed and not transgress"

From here we must learn that we must oppose with self-sacrifice this criminal initiative of evacuating Hebron, as with the saving of the life of a person, concerning which there is a Torah obligation, "You shall not stand by the blood of your fellow." So it is with regard to the danger facing the city of Hebron. This obligation is placed first and foremost on the residents of Hebron, and on all Israel: they must oppose with all the efforts of their strength this destructive plan to destroy the Jewish settlement in Hebron. For it is a continuation of the Arab pogrom against the Jewish settlement in Hebron of the year 5689. And we must give our lives against this malicious scheme of the Government of Israel (which rests on an Arab majority), and be ready to be killed and not to allow the destruction of Hebron, because its law is as a transgression of which they said "let him be killed and not transgress."

This is what I found to answer you on your difficult question. We hope that despite the threats of the government ministers from the left, the Government of Israel will not dare to harm our holy city – historic Hebron, settled by Jews from generation to generation.

With the blessing of the Torah and the redemption,

Rav Shlomo Goren[3]

The words of my teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook zt"l

on the matter of self-sacrifice for the Land of Israel

From section 5 of a proclamation written on 28 Shevat 5734 ('Eretz Ha-Tzvi' p. 23):

With regard to coercion, from whatever side it may be, to make us transgress the laws of the One who chooses His people and His inheritance, blessed be He, we are all commanded with self-sacrifice of "let him be killed and not transgress", "and I shall be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel", even over "the strap of a shoe"; and all the more so over the Torah mitzva of settling and dwelling in the Land of Israel, which in the words of the Sages is equal to all the mitzvot of the Torah.

Section 1 of a proclamation written on 17 Tammuz 5734 ('Eretz Ha-Tzvi' p. 69):

Our clear and absolute self-sacrifice for every part of the land of our life and our holiness, the inheritance of our fathers, our prophecy, our kingdom, our Shekhina, which is obligatory upon us under "let him be killed and not transgress" against any coercion whatsoever, is the foundation and root of the whole Torah, for "the mitzva of dwelling in the Land is a mitzva that includes the whole Torah," in the holy words of the holy Gaon Rabbi Ḥayim ben Attar in the "Or Ha-Ḥayim" at the end of parashat Nitzavim; and this Land belongs to all the myriads of our people, the house of Israel, wherever they are.

notes_en.en: In that same bulletin I wrote an article rejecting the act of Dr Goldstein, while expressing the position that the responsibility for the mad situation that brought a sensitive and pious man to such a terrible act lies on the government, which abandoned the security, the lives and the honour of the Jews of Hebron and the IDF soldiers. Rav Goren too, in a private conversation with me, referred to the act of Dr Goldstein with complete rejection, expressing indignation that he killed Muslims at the time of their prayer.

The dates that Rav Goren wrote were usually civil ones, perhaps with the thought of making it easier for the general public to understand the force of the arguments. Usually I added the Hebrew ones and placed the civil ones in parentheses.
I asked him to expand in explaining his words in this passage, and he dictated to me as follows: "And the words of the Minḥat Ḥinukh (425) are already known, that the mitzva of defending the settlement of the Land overrides the saving of life; and in tractate Shevu'ot 35b it is brought that even a discretionary war overrides the saving of life up to a sixth."

In those days Rav Goren zt"l repeatedly declared several times that he was ready to be killed for the saving of Hebron. In an interview on television too he said this, opening his coat and saying that even if they shot him he would not retreat from his position and would defend Hebron with his body.
However, in my humble opinion, only one who knows that his self-sacrifice will be able to help in a real way in the settling and conquest of the Land is commanded to do so, for he is in the category of "let him be killed and not transgress". But if his actions will not save, it turns out that he was killed and they transgressed. And therefore in practice there is almost no reality in which a Jew will need to be killed for the defence of places in the Land of Israel, except in a war that is organised by the whole of Israel. Likewise, if there should be a prime minister or a minister whose life is threatened if he does not sign or act for withdrawal, the obligation is on him to be killed and not to transgress and hand over parts of the Land of Israel to foreigners. But the simple person – it is almost impossible that he will stand before a situation in which he will need to be killed and not transgress. And see above ch. 3, §4, and also ch. 5, §6. Likewise I remember that at the time of the withdrawal from Yamit, Rav Goren went to persuade those in two shelters – where there was a concern that the Jews barricaded in them intended to be killed and not to be evacuated – that they were forbidden to do so according to halakha. So I heard from him then with my own ears. And indeed he succeeded in persuading those barricaded to be evacuated.
However, with regard to the situation concerning Hebron, Rav Goren's personal self-sacrifice did indeed have an enormous influence. In later days ministers in the government related that his words did indeed act and deterred them from carrying out their scheme.

sections.title_en: Siman 10 – The Attitude to Agreements with the Terror Organisations
sections.body_en:
With God's help, 21 Iyar 5754

2 May 1994

To my great dear one

Rav Eliezer Melamed shlit"a

Secretary of the Rabbis of Yesha

May your peace be abundant for ever,

In your letter of 17 Iyar 5754 you write as follows: Recently the government signed an agreement with Yasser Arafat, head of the murder organisation PLO. And it was agreed that the PLO would act with all its strength to prevent acts of terror against Jews. In practice the "Palestinian Covenant" was not changed, and the acts of terror have increased.

Your question is whether from a moral-halakhic point of view one can at all grant legitimacy to a criminal and murderer, such as the greatest of murderers Yasser Arafat and his organisation of murderers, and sign an agreement with them; or perhaps all the government's signatures are null and void, because the status of the greatest of murderers and his organisation obligates every person who seeks justice and peace to fight him to the end and to punish him with the punishment fitting for him?

Answer: First of all, it must be established that according to the method of the Rambam in chapter 10 (halakha 1) of the Laws of Idolatry, there is a Torah prohibition to make a covenant with the foreigners in the Land of Israel, as it is said (Devarim 7:2): "You shall make no covenant with them, nor show them favour (lo teḥonem)." And although the Rambam at the beginning of his words writes, "One does not make a covenant with the seven nations," from his words in halakha 4 it is clear that this verse comes to forbid also the other nations of the world that are not of the seven nations, as his words there in halakha 4 prove: "For if they have no land, their dwelling is temporary dwelling." And so wrote the author of the book 'Mishneh La-Melekh' in Parashat Derakhim, at the end of Derekh Mitzvotekha, on the method of the Rambam, who holds that the warning "You shall make no covenant with them" includes every foreigner of whatever nation it may be. Although the Semag in negative commandment 47 wrote not to make a covenant with the seven nations, as it is said (Devarim 7:2), "You shall make no covenant with them," but with the other nations making a covenant was not forbidden, as we find with the Giv'onim, to whom they said, "Perhaps you dwell among us, and how shall I make a covenant with you?" (Yehoshua 9:7); and it is written (I Melakhim 5:26): "And there was peace between Ḥiram and Shlomo, and the two of them made a covenant."

And in the Tosafot in Yevamot 23a, s.v. 'hahu', there are two views on this – whether the prohibition "You shall make no covenant with them" applies to all the nations or only to the seven nations. But from the Rambam it is clear that the prohibition is on all the nations, for in chapter 10 of the Laws of Idolatry, halakha 6, the Rambam writes: "All these things are said only at a time when Israel are exiled among the idolaters, or when the hand of the idolaters is strong over Israel; but at a time when the hand of Israel is strong over them, we are forbidden to leave idolaters among us, and even one who dwells temporarily, or passes from place to place with merchandise, shall not pass through our land until he accepts upon himself the seven mitzvot that the sons of Noaḥ were commanded, as it is said: 'They shall not dwell in your land', even for a time. And if he accepted upon himself seven mitzvot, he is a ger toshav. And one accepts a ger toshav only at a time when the Jubilee applies." And so the author of the Ḥinukh holds in mitzva 93, like the Rambam.

And although all the prohibitions seemingly apply, according to the Rambam and the author of the Ḥinukh, to a foreigner who worships idolatry, and according to the method of the Rambam in his responsum to Rabbi Ovadya the convert, responsum 369, the Ishmaelites are not considered idolaters – this does not release the Arabs among us from the prohibition "You shall make no covenant with them, nor show them favour," and it does not permit them to live in the Land. For the Rambam's emphasis is on keeping the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ, among which are included the mitzvot of theft, bloodshed, robbery and dinim, as the Rambam wrote in chapter 9 of the Laws of Kings, halakha 1. And the Arabs of the Land of Israel who are hostile to us and fight against us, especially the terror organisations of the PLO, Hamas, etc., all have the law of idolaters according to the law of the Torah, because they transgress the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ, such as bloodshed, robbery, and dinim, which they do not carry out; therefore their law is as idolaters, who are included in the prohibition of making a covenant and the prohibition of giving them a resting place in the land. And so it is written explicitly in the Sefer Ha-Ḥinukh mentioned above. And for this reason the prohibition of making a covenant exists regarding them also according to the method of the Semag and the Tosafot, because the warning to the foreigners concerning the seven mitzvot of the sons of Noaḥ is their punishment, as the Rambam wrote in chapter 9 of the Laws of Kings.

Conclusion: Therefore, it is clear that the agreement that the Government of Israel made with the greatest of murderers and the murder organisation PLO has no legal validity at all according to the law of the Torah; and the transfer of the sanctified parts of the Land of Israel to the Arabs, according to the agreement with them, is a most severe transgression of the Torah of Israel, for we were commanded "You shall make no covenant with them" and "do not give them a resting place in the land." And everything that the government has done and will do in the so-called peace agreement with the terrorist organisation is all null and void according to halakha and Jewish law; for in any case there will be no peace between us and the Arabs, as the Chief of Staff declared today in the press, saying: "Let us not delude ourselves – the terror will not stop." The Prime Minister makes a covenant with the organisation of murderers while the intifada keeps intensifying, and the bloodshed of Jews does not stop for a single day.

The Prime Minister, Mr Rabin, claimed for years that there is no military solution to the intifada, but a political solution. And now that he has gone for a political solution, handing over half of the Land of Israel to the murderers, the intifada nevertheless keeps intensifying, on the basis of an agreement that the greatest of murderers apparently made with Hamas and other factions of the PLO, that he will take control of territories of the Land of Israel as much as he can, and they will continue to intensify the terror against the Jewish population, as we witness that the blood of Israel is spilled daily like water.

In light of all that has been said, our answer to your question is clear: all the agreements of the minority government that rests on an Arab majority are null and void, and all the government's instructions and arrangements concerning the imaginary peace agreement have no legal or halakhic validity at all; and it is a mitzva to do all that is in our power to frustrate the malicious scheme against the people of Israel and its state, the state of the Jews, by all legal ways.

A day of national mourning: According to the view of the Torah, it is incumbent on the rabbis of Israel to declare Wednesday, 23 Iyar 5754, 4/5/94, on which they are about to sign in Cairo the handing over of parts of the Land of Israel to the terrorists, as a day of national mourning in the Land and in all the dispersions of Israel, of which it is written (Eikha 1:5): "Her adversaries have become the head, her enemies are at ease." "Her princes have become like harts that find no pasture" (there 1:6). And "He has cast down from heaven to earth the beauty of Israel" (there 2:1).

As for the two other questions in your letter, concerning the status of Arafat and the law of such a government, this is not the place nor the hour to answer them.

Rav Shlomo Goren

Former Chief Rabbi of Israel

and Chief Rabbi of the IDF

The words of my teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook zt"l

on the matter of the nullity of agreements that contradict the Torah of Israel

Section 5 of a proclamation written on 14 Elul 5727 (Eretz Ha-Tzvi p. 20):

(After he explained the mitzva of settling the Land and the prohibition of handing over lands to gentiles) "And therefore anything that will be done in this, in contradiction to and in corruption of the wholeness of the Torah of Israel and the strength of the security of Israel, whether through the errors of statesmen or through the hesitations of Torah scholars, is null and void from the outset and for ever, by the power of all Israel, from now and for ever; and all this has no legal or real value, and if they did it, it has no effect. The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Ya'akov is our stronghold, selah."

On the right and duty of rabbis to express the view of the Torah
From the Gaon Rav Avraham Shapira zt"l

After the publication of Rav Goren's words on 'Refusing an Order' (above, siman 5), his words were discussed in the government and in the media, and various personalities demanded to put him on trial. Following this, the Gaon Rav Avraham Shapira zt"l, Chief Rabbi of Israel (5743-5754) and head of the 'Merkaz Ha-Rav' yeshiva, who in those days still served as Chief Rabbi of Israel, went out with a protest and a public statement. His words were published in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin no. 15 of 2 Shevat 5754. And this is his language:

In light of the reports that there was an intention to put the Gaon Rav Shlomo Goren shlit"a on trial for a halakhic opinion that he gave on the matter of evacuating part of the Land of Israel, I hereby express a protest in my name and in the name of the public of rabbis, for the sake of the honour of the Torah.

(a) The steadfast faith of every faithful and upright Jew is that the Torah is above everything that exists in the world, and every problem is examined in the light of the halakha in the Torah of Israel. Whoever does not believe this does not have Jewish faith, for they are our life and the length of our days.

(b) It is the right, and even the duty, of a rabbi in Israel who is authorised to issue instruction in Israel to rule in practice for all who ask him what the view of halakha is on every subject he is asked about, and even to give the opinion of halakha on any law and regulation whatsoever, whether it accords also with the view of halakha. It is the duty of every Torah-observant Jew to refrain from any action that is forbidden according to halakha, even when the action is required by force of law or a government order.

And just as there is a concept of an order that is flagrantly contrary to morality, so, and no less than this, there is a concept of an order that is flagrantly contrary to the law of the Torah.

(c) According to halakha, the obligation of a person in Israel to fulfil the mitzvot of the Torah is above all his obligations towards any civil bodies whatsoever, and even towards the ordinary civil subjection to the orders of the government. And so it is said in the Rambam, Laws of Kings: "If the king decreed to nullify a mitzva, one does not listen to him."

(d) It is explained in the words of the Sages that the Sages said to Nevukhadnetzar: "If for taxes and levies – you are king and your will must be fulfilled; but if for Torah and mitzvot – you and the dog are equal" (Vayikra Rabba 33:6). Heaven forbid that one compare a Jewish government to a foreign government, and all the more so to call them a dog or a poodle. Towards a Jewish government one must express oneself only in a way of honour and importance; but these words of the Sages have as their foundation that one must not obey any government instruction that is flagrantly contrary to the Torah.

All this is part of the foundations of Jewish faith, and this foundation is fluent and rooted in the Jewish people, and it is what sustained the existence of the Jewish nation during thousands of years of the hard and dark exile. An attempt to put a rabbi on trial because he instructed his view in Torah is a terrible blow to the Torah, and may ignite a fire and a severe dispute, which we all seek to avoid.

Never did rabbis agree, because of pressures, to refrain from saying and revealing their view of the Torah and from giving instructions of the Torah on any halakhic problem whatsoever, and they will not be frightened by any threats whatsoever, and all the more so not to change their view. And the author of the Yam Shel Shlomo already wrote (Bava Kamma ch. 4, §9): "… that it is forbidden to alter words of Torah even though there is danger, and one is obligated to give one's life for it… rather we learn from this that we are obligated to give our lives for the sanctification of the Name. And if, heaven forbid, he alters the law, he is like one who denies the Torah of Moshe."

Also the Chief Rabbinate of Israel, from the day of its establishment, never hesitated to publish its view against decisions of the government when this touched on the law of the Torah. Also on the matter of the Land of Israel it decided several times that according to halakha it is forbidden to hand over any part of the Land of Israel into the hands of gentiles; and once a petition was submitted to the High Court of Justice against it, and it was again withdrawn by the petitioner himself, in recognition that this is the task of rabbis, to rule halakhot in practice according to the law of the Torah, and they are obligated to reveal their view in public.

All this I wrote also in the name of many rabbis in the Land who asked me, as a former Chief Rabbi, to protest publicly against the desecration of the honour of the Torah by threats against rabbis who give a halakhic opinion.[1]

notes_en.en:
I will further add from the words of the Gaon Rav Avraham Shapira zt"l, brought in the book 'Morasha' – a collection of talks and articles, pp. 13-14, where he proved and explained the standing of the Sages in assessing reality, from Pesaḥim 56a. There it is related that King Ḥizkiyahu did six things; for three they agreed with him and for three they did not agree with him. Some of the things are purely halakhic, such as that he intercalated Nisan in Nisan. But some of them are connected to policy, such as that he stopped up the waters of the upper Giḥon, and cut off the doors of the Temple and sent them to the king of Ashur. And we learn that the Sages have a position regarding political acts. And in the Tur and Shulḥan Arukh YD 251:14 it is ruled, following the responsa of the Rosh (beginning of rule 6, 1-2), that one may change even money that was dedicated to Torah study for public needs in order to bribe the ruler. And the reason is explained in the Bei'ur Ha-Gra, s.k. 24: as Ḥizkiyahu did, who gave the sacred property of Heaven to the kings of the nations of the world. And it is difficult: this is one of the acts that Ḥizkiyahu did for which they did not agree with him; if so, why did they rule the halakha like Ḥizkiyahu? One must say that the Rosh and the Gra hold that the Sages too agree that if there is a need, then it is permitted to give the sacred property of the Temple to a gentile king in order to bribe him; only that they held that at that time there was no need for it, and for this they did not agree with him. And likewise regarding stopping up the waters of the Giḥon: Ḥizkiyahu stopped them in order to withhold water from the army of Ashur if it should come to besiege Jerusalem, whereas the Sages held that there was no need for it. Thus the Sages have standing in assessing reality. And since prophecy departed, this is the task of the Sages, as brought in Seder Olam Rabba ch. 30: "Since prophecy departed, incline your ear to hear the words of the Sages."
And so it is proved in Berakhot 3b, regarding a decision to go out to battle: after David would instruct his men to go out to battle, they would consult with the military experts, such as Aḥitofel, and afterwards they would take counsel with the Sanhedrin, who are the Sages. That is, after the logical consideration they still need to hear what the view of the Sages is on this consideration. And only afterwards would they ask of the Urim and Tummim; and without consulting the Sanhedrin they would also not be answered by the Urim and Tummim (and see Rashi there).

sections.title_en: Siman 13 – Responsum on the Expulsion of Jews
sections.body_en:
Responsum on the Expulsion of Jews
From our teacher and master
Rav Avraham Shapira
Head of the Merkaz Ha-Rav yeshiva and Chief Rabbi of Israel 5743-5753

The responsum was written in the summer of 5765, before the expulsion of the Jews from Gush Katif and northern Shomron and the destruction of their homes and settlements at the hands of the Sharon government, which will be remembered for this with abhorrence.

Menaḥem Av, the days of Bein Ha-Metzarim 5765

Responsum on the matter of the expulsion of Jews

In answer to your questions on the matter of the expulsion of the Jews from Gush Katif in order to hand this region of the Land over to gentiles. One ought to expand at length on each and every section, as is the way of Torah, and especially in these important matters; but for now I will answer you briefly, with practical settled halakha, so that the house of Israel may know the way of the Torah and the mitzva in which they should walk.

(a) According to the law of the Torah there is a complete prohibition to hand over land of Israel to a gentile, because of the negative commandment "lo teḥonem" and because of the nullification of the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel, which obligates each and every individual of Israel. This prohibition applies to every Jew – civilian and soldier alike. An order to take part in the evacuation of Jews from their home in order to hand the land over to gentiles is an order that contradicts the religion of our holy Torah, and it is forbidden to carry it out. Any order that contradicts halakha and compels one to transgress words of Torah has no validity whatsoever; it is forbidden to obey it, and no person has the authority to give it. Concerning such a case the Rambam wrote: "Needless to say, if the king decreed to nullify a mitzva, one does not listen to him" (Laws of Kings 3:9). Whoever transgresses this prohibition will not be held guiltless, neither in this world nor in the World to Come.

(b) Included in the prohibition of handing over land to gentiles is a prohibition to assist those engaged in the transgression. Therefore one must not block the road to Gush Katif or assist in any other way in the expulsion of the Jews from their homes. Likewise, a soldier called up for reserve duty must refrain from reporting if his service is intended to enable other soldiers to engage in the transgression.

(c) A soldier or policeman who harms the sacred things of Israel and, heaven forbid, destroys objects of Heaven and articles of holiness, such as Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot, whether this is done in the course of the transgression of the evacuation or not, disgraces the sacred things of Israel and transgresses the negative commandment "You shall not do so to the Lord your God."

(d) One who demolishes anything of a synagogue is like one who demolishes a stone of the Sanctuary (Mordekhai, chapter Benei Ha-Ir, and Magen Avraham 152, s.k. 6). There is an absolute prohibition on any soldier or policeman to take part in the demolition of a synagogue or a beit midrash. Included in this is the destruction of the furnishings of the synagogue, which are like the synagogue itself (Bei'ur Halakha, siman 152). Woe to him and woe to the soul of a soldier or policeman who takes part in this sin.

(e) A soldier or policeman who damages the property of the settlers is a robber. There is no "dina de-malkhuta" here, but rather the extortion of a government that transgresses the law of the Torah (Shakh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 73, s.k. 39). It is the right of every person to defend his property from harm or damage done not in accordance with halakha.

(f) Every Jew must do all that is in his power to prevent the transgression. Likewise, there is an obligation of protest on each and every Jew. Of course, one must not take violent measures against IDF soldiers or Israel Police officers.

(g) Only the greatest Torah scholars of the generation, whose strength is to rule on grave questions in all parts of the Torah and whose rulings are accepted in Israel, are fit to rule on these questions that concern the whole of Israel. Whoever has not reached this level must refrain from ruling on these matters; and if he nonetheless issues halakhic rulings, the Rambam already applied to him (Laws of Torah Study 5:4): "a wicked man, a fool and arrogant; and about him it is said: 'For she has cast down many wounded', etc.; and about him it is said: 'And mighty are all her slain' – these are the minor students who have not acquired Torah properly and seek to make themselves great before the ignorant and among the people of their city, and they jump up and sit at the head to judge and to rule in Israel. They are the ones who increase dispute, and they are the ones who destroy the world and extinguish the lamp of Torah and ruin the vineyard of the Lord of hosts. About them Shlomo said in his wisdom: 'Catch us the foxes, the little foxes that ruin the vineyards.'"

(h) Those who act in practice according to what rabbis who have not reached the level of instruction on these subjects ruled for them (as explained in the section above) are not in the category of unwitting transgressors, and they too will in the future have to give an account (see Pitḥei Teshuva, Even Ha-Ezer 17, s.k. 140, and Pitḥei Teshuva YD siman 99, s.k. 5, in the name of the early Tzemaḥ Tzedek).

From the straits, in the days of Bein Ha-Metzarim: may the Lord hearken to the voice of His people and answer us with expansiveness, and out of distress and sorrow bring about for us redemption and relief, and remove the reproach of His people from all the earth, for the Lord has spoken.

Siman 14
Rav Naḥum Eliezer Rabinovitch
Head of the 'Birkat Moshe' yeshiva in Ma'ale Adumim
and author of the work 'Yad Peshuta' on the Rambam
Explaining the halakhic ruling
that forbids the evacuation of IDF bases in Judea, Samaria and Gaza

Rav Rabinovitch was among the partners to the ruling published in Tammuz 5755, which was brought above, 5:8, page 120. In this responsum, which has two parts, Rav Rabinovitch explained his view. The first part, dealing with pikuaḥ nefesh (saving life), was printed in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin no. 27 of Elul 5755, and the second part, dealing with the mitzva of settling the Land, was printed in bulletin no. 28.

As you requested, I will try to survey briefly the halakhic considerations that moved me to hold on to the hem of the cloak of the great rabbis who issued the famous ruling, and chiefly what the reason was for publishing the ruling. Likewise one must relate to several claims that were voiced publicly against the ruling.

The discussion divides essentially into two: in the first part we will discuss the practical application of the ruling and why there was a necessity to publish it now; the second part deals with a fundamental problem, which goes far beyond this ruling and also beyond certain particular halakhot.

Pikuaḥ nefesh
We all remember the sad case of that reserve soldier who travelled through Ramallah to report for duty, and erred and took a wrong turn. He did not go fifty metres from the main road, and a wild mob fell upon him. All this happened at a time when there are IDF patrols on the main road. What will happen, heaven forbid, if the IDF leaves the city and abandons the road? What will happen to the people of Pesagot, Ofra and Beit El, and the other settlements, for whom the Ramallah road is a vital artery? If the roads today are presumed dangerous, then if the IDF leaves there, the danger will be tangible and certain. The blood of the terrible murder in Ma'ale Mikhmash has not yet dried, and there is no doubt that the talk of removing the IDF contributed its part to encouraging the murderer to enter the settlement.

There are those who claimed that one may not raise an argument of pikuaḥ nefesh without consulting experts, and brought a parable of a sick person about whom one asks the doctor whether he is in danger and Shabbat must be desecrated for him. Perhaps such a claim has a place when one is speaking of overall policy – that is, whether this or that agreement will prevent bloodshed or not. This is like an illness that is unknown to us, and one must ask a doctor who does know. But if a person is drowning in the sea before your eyes, and you know how to swim – at such a time does one run to the doctor to ask whether there is danger here? In a matter whose danger is clear to every person of understanding, one who goes to ask an expert before acting to rescue – about him the Sages said: one who asks is shedding blood. And so the Rambam ruled (Laws of Shabbat 2:17): "And whoever hastens to rescue is praiseworthy, and he need not take permission from the court in any matter that involves danger."

When one is speaking of the departure of the IDF and the abandonment of the roads, it is clear as the sun at noon that there is a certain and immediate danger to thousands of Jews, and there is no place to hand over such a decision to any experts. And even if all the experts were of one mind that the political move will in the end bring about the saving of lives in the long term – even in such a case the matter is no more than a doubt, especially as the military experts are divided in their opinion – and a long-term doubt does not override a certain immediate danger.

To what may the matter be compared? A person is drowning in the sea, and the experts say that there are sharks there, and if they eat the drowning man and fill their bellies, then they will not endanger the bathers who go down to the sea at that time. Would it enter one's mind that in order to prevent the danger facing those who will go down to the sea afterwards we should refrain and not save the drowning man? Surely it is clear that one who refrains from saving the drowning man is shedding blood. It is a great principle that a saving of life in the future does not override a danger to life now. The words of the Rambam (Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 5:5) are clear: "If gentiles said to them, 'Give us one of you and we will kill him, and if not, we will kill all of you', let them all be killed, and let them not hand over to them a single soul of Israel."

The claim that in matters of security and danger only the government has authority to decide is out of place, since one is speaking of a situation that is evident to all.

For this reason there is also an obligation to publish the ruling in good time, in order to prevent the danger before it comes. For the Sages said that in pikuaḥ nefesh "one who asks is shedding blood, and the one who is asked is disgraceful." That is, the Sage whom people come to ask – upon him lies the responsibility to publish and to make known publicly that pikuaḥ nefesh overrides the whole Torah (except for three transgressions) before a real threat occurs, so that one who finds himself in such a situation will know at once what to do and will not delay until he goes to ask. And if he did not make this known in advance, he is disgraceful.

Of course, once it is clear to all that one is speaking of a certain and recognised danger, all the other arguments raised against the ruling are pointless. For example, those who said that because of the 'ruling' there will be those who want to dismantle the hesder yeshivot. And others said that it will hold up the promotion of religious officers. And other such trivial claims – as if there were any consideration at all that stands against saving lives! Would it enter one's mind that it should be permitted to endanger lives in order to enable the promotion of religious officers in the army?!

The mitzva of settling the Land of Israel
There is one who tried to blur the impression the halakhic ruling made by raising claims against the matter of settling the Land of Israel. Indeed, the ruling was declared specifically in the form in which it was declared in order to prevent immediate bloodshed. But it is clear that in the background of the matter there stands also a fundamental consideration, expressed in the subject of settling the Land of Israel. However, it must be stated clearly that even if the halakha is not like the Ramban z"l, who counts the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel as a positive commandment, this does not diminish the importance of the matter of the Land of Israel. On the contrary, the matter becomes much more severe. I have already written elsewhere that the Rambam, who does not count the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel among the 613, does not disagree with the Ramban on any particular law concerning the obligation of settling the Land; on the contrary, he rules as halakha all the obligations that the Sages listed regarding settling the Land, and states clearly that they are binding also in our time.

The Rambam explains that there is an obligation more comprehensive and deeper than a mitzva counted among the 613: an obligation that flows from a principle that the Torah presents as a foundation for the mitzvot. In the fifth root of his introduction to the Sefer Ha-Mitzvot, the Rambam writes that one does not count the reason for a mitzva as a mitzva.

This rule has implications for all the foundations of the Torah and faith. The purpose of all the mitzvot is either to instil true beliefs or to rectify the life of the individual and society. But concerning several of these principles we were not commanded particular mitzvot. For example, there is no mitzva among the 613 to believe that the Holy One, blessed be He, knows the deeds of human beings and searches their hearts. But it is clear that one who denies God's knowledge of the deeds of human beings denies the whole Torah, and removes the basis of all the mitzvot. In this he removes himself from the community of Israel. Likewise, there is no negative commandment in the Torah forbidding one to damage another's property. Indeed, the Torah establishes an obligation to pay for damages even if one damaged unwittingly, even under duress, and even if one's property did the damage; but an explicit prohibition there is not.

Would it enter one's mind that by Torah law it is permitted to damage the property of another? Certainly not. If so, what is the source of the prohibition? The Rambam explains that one of the fundamental purposes of the Torah is the rectification of society and the prevention of injustice. This principle is anchored in many verses.

The distinction between a purpose and a mitzva is this, that both are a source of obligations: an obligation that flows from a mitzva counted among the 613 is generally defined, specific and limited, for that is the characteristic of a mitzva. But a purpose, or "the reason for a mitzva", is different from the mitzva itself. The purposes are comprehensive and sweeping, and many paths lead to attaining the purpose, and likewise many factors prevent its realisation. Since the Torah has informed us that this purpose is His will, blessed be He, it follows as a matter of course that we are obligated to act in every possible way to advance the purpose. And the same applies in reverse: one must refrain, beware and guard oneself from any action that could cause the attainment of the purpose to fail, and one must likewise act to remove possible obstacles. And everything depends on the time, the place and the possibilities.

It turns out that there is an enormous difference between the scope of the actions required by a mitzva counted among the 613 and those founded on a purpose that the Torah established. Unlike a mitzva, which is limited and defined in its scope, the purpose creates obligations incomparably broader and deeper.

Among the purposes that the Torah dictates to us, an honoured place is kept for the Land of Israel. Many verses testify that the reason and purpose of many mitzvot is to bring us to the Land of Israel: "And now, Israel, hearken to the statutes and to the ordinances… that you may live, and go in and possess the land" (Devarim 4:1). "And you shall keep His statutes and His commandments… that it may go well with you and with your children after you, and that you may prolong your days upon the land which the Lord your God gives you" (there, 40). "And you shall do what is right and good in the eyes of the Lord, that it may go well with you, and that you may go in and possess the good land" (there 6:18).

From now on, knowledge is easy for one who understands that all the particular halakhot concerning settling the Land of Israel are anchored in this purpose. And not only the particular halakhot mentioned in the Talmud and ruled by the Rambam; rather, at every time and in every age we are obligated to do every activity that advances the purpose of giving us the Land as an inheritance. And so too in reverse: every action that lessens our hold on the Land or distances Jews from the tracts of our soil is absolutely forbidden, and it is like denial of the holy Torah, which testifies that His will, blessed be He, is that His people dwell in its land. And about this it is said: "And they despised the desirable land; they did not believe His word" (Tehillim 106:24) – so these two matters are equivalent.

According to this it is well understood that also with regard to punishment, one who transgresses and causes the purpose of the Torah to fail is more severe than one who transgresses a particular mitzva of the 613. The punishments for the mitzvot are also defined and explicit, and one may not add to them. But one who uproots the purposes of the Torah deserves the punishment of a rebel. Our great master expands on this in several places (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 11:3, and Guide of the Perplexed 3:41, and elsewhere). Therefore it is stated explicitly in the verse about their despising the desirable land: "Therefore He said that He would destroy them, had not Moshe His chosen stood before Him in the breach, to turn back His wrath from destroying" (Tehillim 106:23).

This explains the view of the Rambam, who did not count settling the Land of Israel in the number of the mitzvot: because this duty is broader and more severe even than the severe mitzvot, and it is not possible at all to encompass and exhaust it within the definitions of a particular mitzva.[1]

However, here there is room for a litigant to argue in defence of some of those who disagree. Since in this matter of settling the Land of Israel there is no fixed and standing definition, but rather we are obligated in every action that contributes to advancing and establishing our settlement, it turns out that the matter depends on the assessment of the political and military situation. Consequently a certain situation is possible, as in war, in which in order to survive one must shorten the lines and reduce the fronts in order to prevent defeat, as Yisrael Saba, our father Ya'akov, did: "then the camp that is left shall escape." According to this approach, there are those who have claimed that in order to prevent wars in the future, and in order to secure the foundations of the state, one must reach an agreement with the murderers and concede to them part of the Land so that we may be able to survive in the rest. If so, there is no transgression in the agreement of surrender; on the contrary, it is the necessity of reality. The weak one has no choice but must save what can be saved. Even though they said: "The beginning of a fall is flight," what shall one do who has no strength to stand against a force stronger than he?

However, even this claim has no place when the matter involves an immediate transgression of abandoning the lives of Jews. And it has already been explained above that one may not hand over even one person to death in order to save many. It is a great principle in the Torah that the end does not sanctify the means. Even if the matter were clear and agreed that a contract with Satan would bring true peace and the saving of many lives in the future, even then it would be forbidden to do it at the cost of the shedding of the blood of Jews now.

With this we return to our conclusion in the first part: one who abandons the lives of Israel, even in order to save with certainty the lives of others in the future, is shedding blood. All the more so when the saving in the future is in great doubt, and the chances of saving lives in the future are very slim. It seems to me that after two years of the imaginary "peace", and hundreds of victims of the "peace" who were murdered and thousands who were wounded, even if Jerusalem be searched with candles, there will not be found people with open eyes who still support the nightmarish hallucination of "Arafat's peace".

The conclusion that emerges is that every God-fearing person is obligated in these days to stand firm and to act with all his strength for the deepening of our hold on the Land and the fortification of our positions: "Be strong, and let us strengthen ourselves for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the Lord do what is good in His eyes."
