Before Rav Goren's letter we will set out a proclamation written by my teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Kook zt"l on 27 Shevat 5737, and published in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin no. 21 (Le-Netivot Yisrael, vol. 2, Beit El edition, p. 282).

Clarifying matters concerning the Temple Mount
My teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook zt"l

All the great halakhic stringency of the prohibition of entering it, because we are still, according to halakha, in a state of impurity, does not touch, harm or diminish in any way the value of our proprietary ownership of the area of this holy place, glorious in holiness. Our honourable Chief of Staff, Mr Mordekhai Gur, merited – and with him and above him the honourable our teacher and master the Gaon Rabbi Shlomo Goren, head of the rabbis of Israel – that through them this place was liberated from the rule of the gentiles, and it too, like all the areas of the places of the Land of our life and holiness, is in our possession and ownership. In our possession and ownership they arrange there for themselves their order of prayers on Friday. Groups of our soldiers who are there guard and supervise them by order of our authorities. Even if we are careful about entering there, according to the measure of halakha, within this and out of this our ownership of the whole area of this place stands fixed and enduring in all its force, as does our permission for this presence of the gentiles there, who are in no way the owners of this place.

Words I wrote on the view of Rav Tzvi Yehuda (from Revivim: 'The Chief Rabbi's War over the Temple Mount' – 20 Marḥeshvan 5775; 'The Mitzva of Inheriting the Land on the Temple Mount' – 27 Marḥeshvan 5775)

It seems to my humble opinion that if my teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook zt"l had seen that the excessive caution about going up onto the Mount was bringing about the loss of sovereignty and the turning of the Mount into a focus of hatred against Israel, he would have agreed with the words of Rav Goren that it is permitted and a mitzva to go up. It further seems to my humble opinion that he would have relied on Rav Goren's halakhic clarifications regarding the places that are permitted for entry.

They asked: on what basis do I write this? Is it not known that Rav Tzvi Yehuda lent his support to the warning of the Chief Rabbinate not to go up onto the Temple Mount, out of concern for entering the holy place without purity?

Answer: My words are based on studying his words. According to what he wrote in the proclamation, sovereignty was for him the principal of principals, since the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel obligates us that the Land be in our hands and not in the hands of another nation – and all the more so the Temple Mount, which is the most sanctified place in all the Land of Israel. And all of Rav Tzvi Yehuda's words were said at a time when sovereignty was clear and settled, as we have seen how much trouble he took to detail the marks of sovereignty and rule over the Temple Mount.

And had he heard that following Arab riots and various pressures, from within and without, the flag of Israel no longer waves over the Temple Mount, and the permanent police post has been removed from there, and there is no longer a permanent military presence on the Mount, and police and soldiers are not permitted to enter the mosque, and the Arabs no longer merely "arrange there for themselves their prayers on Friday", but rather from there calls of incitement against Israel go out to the whole world, and Arab youths dare to mock and curse police and soldiers, and the Arabs hold parties and football games there and bury their dead there while displaying contempt towards the State of Israel, and all the Jews who go up onto the Temple Mount enter by permission of the Waqf and with their close escort, while gangs of Arabs curse and revile them – had our master heard all this he would have shuddered with pain and supported every kosher means within the framework of halakha to strengthen sovereignty over the Temple Mount. It should be noted that in the merit of the Jews going up onto the Mount in recent years, the marks of sovereignty are gradually returning.

One can further see from the wording of the proclamation Rav Tzvi Yehuda's attitude to Rav Goren and to his halakhic authority, and from this I could deduce that he would have relied on his halakhic clarifications.

* *

The letter of the Gaon Rav Shlomo Goren
A connection of many years existed between Rav Goren and Yitzḥak Rabin. Rav Goren was the Chief Rabbi of the IDF, and Yitzḥak Rabin advanced up the ladder of command until in the Six-Day War he served as Chief of Staff. The Oslo agreements, made by Yitzḥak Rabin during his term as Prime Minister, greatly depressed Rav Goren. His pain over Yitzḥak Rabin's actions was unbearable. He attacked his policy and called for demonstrations against it. He called on soldiers to refuse orders. Rabin was angry at Rav Goren's statements. Several times he criticised his words at cabinet meetings, and government figures even issued threats that they would put him on trial for sedition. Nevertheless a personal connection remained between them, and Rav Goren did not despair of sounding the alarm; and when he thought there was room to turn to Yitzḥak Rabin with a direct appeal, he wrote this letter. Rav Goren sent me a copy of it so that I would publish it as an article in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin. Indeed I edited it in the form of an article and published it in bulletin no. 21 in Elul 5754. Here the letter is brought in its original form, as Rav Goren sent it to the Prime Minister Yitzḥak Rabin:

I once asked Rav Goren how personalities who had been partners in the liberation of Judea, Samaria and Gaza agree so easily to give up Judea and Samaria. He answered: they never wanted to conquer Judea and Samaria; Heaven brought it about that they conquered against their will. Another time I asked him whether Rabin could be defined as an "okher Yisrael" (troubler of Israel). He answered: certainly, and added that to a certain extent Aḥav, about whom Eliyahu said that he was the "troubler of Israel", was better than him, because Aḥav guarded the honour of Israelite nationhood more. Nevertheless they treated each other with a certain respect. On 24 Marḥeshvan 5755, three months after this letter was written, Rav Goren passed away, and the Prime Minister Mr Rabin cleared time from his busy schedule and came with his wife to console Rav Goren's family.

On the matter of the Temple Mount: immediately after the liberation of the Mount in the Six-Day War, Rav Goren wanted to establish a beit midrash of the military rabbinate on the Temple Mount, in a place permitted for entry, in order to draw closer to the holy and to express the sovereignty of the people of Israel over the Temple Mount. And he even held classes and talks there. However, government ministers demanded that he be taken down from the Mount, and he was forced to retreat from his plan. Afterwards he received a place for a synagogue in the Maḥkama building, part of which is within the Temple Mount, and there he would hold regular prayers on Yom Kippur and Tisha Be-Av. Since part of the synagogue is on the Temple Mount, he instituted a special order of prayer there, as was customary at the time when the Temple stood. When the ḥazan concludes a blessing, for example the first blessing of the Amida, instead of saying "Blessed are You, Hashem, Shield of Avraham", he says "Blessed are You, Hashem, God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting; blessed are You, Hashem, Shield of Avraham". And the congregation does not say "Barukh hu u-varukh shemo", but at the end of the blessing, instead of "Amen", they say "Blessed be the Name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever". Likewise he instituted prostration with the hands and feet stretched out, and without spreading a cloth on the floor, according to the law of the Temple Mount. Today too the minyan continues to be held in the same place according to the same rules, with Rav Goren's son coordinating the arrangements of the minyan and Rav Yisrael Ariel leading the prayer.

Towards the end of his days, when he saw that the Arabs were increasingly taking control of the Mount, he again encouraged going up onto the Temple Mount to the permitted places after immersion, and for this purpose he published his book 'Har Ha-Bayit'.

With God's help, 17 Av 5754

25 July 1994

To the honourable Prime Minister and Minister of Defence

Mr Yitzḥak Rabin

May your peace be abundant.

I find it a duty of the soul to respond to the publications heard from the mouth of your Foreign Minister, that there is a plan to compromise with King Hussein on giving King Hussein a sovereign foothold on the Temple Mount, and thereby to win the heart of the Hashemite king, who claims ownership of Jerusalem and the holy places.

I wish to inform you hereby that the Temple Mount is considered the holy of holies of the Jewish nation,[9] and let them not deceive you with fabricated stories that in any case Jews are forbidden to go up and pray on the Temple Mount. I enclose for you herewith my book "Har Ha-Bayit", which I published two years ago, and in it about 12 maps in which I delimited the boundaries of the places on the Temple Mount that Jews are forbidden to go up to, and the areas where Jews are permitted to go up and pray. From the maps it is proven that most of the Temple Mount is permitted according to halakha for entry by Jews. And in my aforementioned book I establish where a synagogue could be built there for Jews to pray.

We have no intentions whatsoever of preventing the Muslims from going up onto the Temple Mount and praying in their mosques; we demand that the open areas of the Temple Mount, where there are no mosques and which are under the open sky, be left under Jewish sovereignty, and that Jews be allowed to pray there as they wish.

From the destruction of the Second Temple until three hundred years ago, the prayer of the Jews on the Temple Mount did not cease:

(a) With the destruction of the Second Temple, Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi of Israel, set up his chamber on the steps of the Temple Mount, and from there Torah went forth to Israel, as explained in tractate Sanhedrin (11b). Likewise Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel set up his academy on a step of the Temple Mount (tractate Avoda Zara 20a).

(b) On fast days there were special texts of prayer to be said on the Temple Mount with the blowing of the shofar, as explained in tractate Ta'anit 15b: "And when the matter came before the Sages, they said: We were accustomed to do so only at the Eastern Gate and on the Temple Mount."

(c) The traveller from Bordeaux (fourth century) relates: "And the Jews come once a year (on 9 Av) to this place (the Temple Mount) and weep and lament by one stone that remained there from their Temple, and they anoint it with oil" (see Tziyon journal, book 3, 5689, from p. 111 on, the article of Yehuda Yitzḥak Yeḥezkel).

(d) R. Avraham bar Ḥiyya Ha-Nasi (12th century) describes the "house of prayer and study" that existed for the Jews on the Temple Mount, in his words: "And likewise the kings of Ishmael used to treat them well and permitted Israel to come to the Temple Mount and build on it a house of prayer and study, and all the exiles of Israel near the House used to go up to it on festivals and appointed times and pray within it, and set their prayer corresponding to the tamid and musaf offerings." (See the great article of Professor B. Z. Dinur, 'A House of Prayer and Study for the Jews on the Temple Mount in the Days of the Arabs', the aforementioned Tziyon journal, from p. 4 on.)

(e) The Rambam, when he went up to Jerusalem in the month of Sivan 4926 (1165), prayed in the house of prayer on the Temple Mount. So it emerges from the letter of the Rambam brought in the book Ḥaredim, Sha'ar Teshuva, ch. 4. (See on this too the aforementioned article of Dinur, p. 87, note 178, and the article of Yeḥezkel, pp. 107-114.)

(f) The great traveller R. Binyamin of Tudela, who stayed about two years in Jerusalem in the 12th century, describes the prayer of the Jews before the dome of the Foundation Stone.

(g) Still in the 16th century, in the days of the Radbaz – R. David ben Zimra – "everyone was accustomed to go up on those ascents (onto the Temple Mount) to see from there the whole House, and we did not hear or see anyone who protested against them" (Responsa of the Radbaz, part 1, siman 691).

I do not wish to discuss here the halakhic aspects of entering the Temple Mount; for us it suffices to remember that the Rambam, who is considered stringent on this subject, prayed there himself – and what shall we answer after him?

The uniqueness of the "Western Wall" as a place of prayer for Jews is new from a historical point of view, and does not exceed three hundred years. Its beginning dates from the decrees and restrictions that the Muslim rulers imposed on the Jews, and the abolition of the "synagogue and house of study" that had existed for hundreds of years on the Temple Mount. But in no way whatsoever does the Wall, whose entire sanctity is in that it borders the Temple Mount, have the right to be a substitute for the Mount of the Lord. For the Western Wall about which it is said in the Midrash (Shemot Rabba 2:2), "The Shekhina never moves from the Western Wall", means the western wall of the Holy of Holies or of the Azara in the Temple, and not the wall of the Temple Mount (and this has already been clarified by us in the book Har Ha-Bayit). The prayers by the Wall symbolise the exile of the people and its expulsion from the Temple Mount, and our prayers on the Temple Mount symbolise the return of the people to its Land and to the place of its Temple.

The rabbis who, out of lack of topographical and halakhic knowledge of the Temple Mount, are afraid to go up and pray on the Temple Mount may be stringent with themselves; but for us and for the whole people free prayer on the Temple Mount must be made possible in the permitted areas after immersion in a pure mikve, and the Muslims must be given free access to their mosques on the Temple Mount – but heaven forbid to hand over to the Waqf or to King Hussein sovereignty over the whole Temple Mount.

And let the king not feed you with disinformation that he was always the ruler over the Temple Mount. This claim has no basis, for in the days of the British Mandate Hussein and Transjordan had no foothold whatsoever in Jerusalem and on the Temple Mount; and just as he took control by force of the West Bank in the War of Independence, so he took control by force of Jerusalem and the Temple Mount. And Hussein's claim has no foothold whatsoever in international documents – he ruled both in Judea and Samaria and in Jerusalem as a foreign occupier, and no body with international authority granted him any status in the West Bank. So too two presidents of the United States, Mr Carter and Mr Reagan, admitted before me at my meeting with them in the White House.

We have no objection whatsoever to King Hussein going up to the Temple Mount to pray in the mosques; but he must not be granted rights of sovereignty over the Temple Mount, and he must not be allowed to hang an Arab flag on the mosques, as the previous Prime Minister, Mr Menaḥem Begin z"l, promised me, as you will see from his letter addressed to me, enclosed herewith.

Handing over the Temple Mount to a foreign ruler means abandoning the holy of holies of the nation into the hands of foreigners, for which there will never be atonement.

For the Muslims the Temple Mount itself has no sanctity: they do not remove their shoes on entering the Temple Mount, and only on entering the mosques do they remove their shoes, whereas the Jews were commanded to remove their shoes on entering the Temple Mount, as we learned in tractate Berakhot chapter 9, mishna 5: "One may not enter the Temple Mount with his staff or with his shoes." And so the Rambam rules in the Laws of the Chosen House, chapter 7, halakhot 1-2: "It is a positive commandment to revere the Sanctuary, as it is said: 'And you shall revere My Sanctuary.' A person may not enter the Temple Mount with his staff or with the shoes on his feet." It is implied from the Rambam that the whole Temple Mount has the status of a Sanctuary, which is not so for the Muslims, for whom the Temple Mount itself has no pre-eminence of sanctity.

Therefore I must inform you that we must give our lives for preserving Jewish sovereignty over the Temple Mount, for it constitutes the summit of the ten sanctities of the Land of Israel. And in no way whatsoever will we give up our right to pray on the Temple Mount under the open sky in the areas permitted for entry.

I hope that in any negotiation with Hussein, King of Jordan, and with other international bodies, you will stand with all your strength for our rights on Mount Moriah, which was sanctified from the days of King David, when he bought the threshing floor of Aravna the Jebusite on Mount Moriah and built there an altar to the Lord, as he was commanded by Gad the prophet, as stated (II Shmuel 24:18-25): "And Gad came that day to David and said to him: Go up, rear an altar to the Lord in the threshing floor of Aravna the Jebusite… And David built there an altar to the Lord, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings; and the Lord was entreated for the land…"

I hope that at the time of decision you will know how to stand with strength and might not to hand over the Temple Mount into the hands of foreigners.

With blessing and esteem,

Rav Shlomo Goren

Former Chief Rabbi of Israel

and Chief Rabbi of the IDF

Here is the place to add words that I wrote in the Rabbis of Yesha bulletin no. 23 of Tevet 5755:

Question: What should be the attitude towards the Temple Mount, the place of our Temple? Has the time not come to begin wide public action for the building of the Temple? Answer: In my humble opinion there are two aspects to our relationship with the Temple Mount: from the side of general Israelite nationhood, that is, from the side of the holiness of the people and the Land; and from the Divine side, that is, the building of the Temple. From the national side it is fitting for us to emphasise to a greater degree our connection to the Temple Mount; but we have not yet reached the supreme Divine level of the Temple, and therefore it is not relevant today to act directly for the building of the Temple or the offering of sacrifices.

The service of the Temple is a lofty and supreme thing, and in order to reach it one must rise in spiritual-national level, in faith, in Torah and in mitzvot. The Temple is the peak of Israel's perfection in the service of God, and one must not jump to the summit before building the foundational steps. According to Rashi the Temple will descend from heaven, whereas according to the Rambam human beings will build it. And the Ramak explains that first its sanctity and the indwelling of the Shekhina of the Temple will be revealed from heaven, as Rashi says, and afterwards, as a framework for the revelation of the Shekhina, we will build the Temple with our hands, as the Rambam holds. But in our present situation we must progress and pass through several more stages until we are worthy of the light of the Third Temple being revealed upon the Mount. Certainly the Holy One, blessed be He, can pour upon us a spirit from on high and bring us back to Him in complete repentance in a short time, and then of course we will build the Temple. But we on our part, in our present situation, cannot jump to building the Temple. And the work on behalf of the Temple – that is, on behalf of the open indwelling of His Shekhina and the sanctification of God's Name among us – must be done through delving deeply into Torah, mending the relations between a person and his fellow, and rising in the fulfilment of the mitzvot. And everyone who acts for the building of the nation in the light of the Torah places a further course in the building of the Third Temple. Indeed, exceptional individuals are commanded to engage in the matters of the Temple service in depth and breadth, in order to pave the way for all of us for the continuation of the ascent; but the main open public work must be directed towards increasing faith and mending the relations between a person and his fellow.

But from the national aspect, there is no doubt that all of us need to feel a much stronger connection to the place of our Temple, the joy of our life. Indeed, from a spiritual aspect it is still hard for us to feel a great yearning for the Temple service; we have not yet risen to this level of holiness (for this one needs to study the general matter of the Temple and its service). But it is impossible that the most sanctified place of our people should be neglected by us. It is the place where Yitzḥak was bound, and around it David established our capital city. To it all Israel looked on Yom Kippur at the time of the service of the High Priest, and in it was the Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the Great Sanhedrin sat, and from there instructions went out to all Israel; and all Israel would go up to it three times a year for close to a thousand years. How is it possible that this place should be abandoned by us? Any other people that had such a place would fight for it with self-sacrifice. And how do we forget its greatness and holiness, and let enemies and haters do in it whatever they please? Every Jew with a sense of loyalty to his people and his homeland, who is connected to the general ideals of the people of Israel, is obligated to act in all effective ways for Israel's rule over the Temple Mount.[10]

* *

Rav Goren's war over the Temple Mount

(Words I wrote in Revivim, 20 Marḥeshvan 5775)

Rav Goren's decision to print the book on the Temple Mount

Next week, on 24 Marḥeshvan, twenty years will have passed since the passing of the Chief Rabbi of Israel, the Gaon Rav Shlomo Goren zt"l. In these days, when the Temple Mount is being discussed, it is fitting to recall things from his book 'Har Ha-Bayit', which he published about a year before his passing. In his book he clarifies at length the location of the Temple and the courtyards, the places forbidden for entry even after immersion and the places permitted for entry after immersion.

Those were the days of Rabin's second government, which made agreements with the terror organisation PLO and handed over parts of the Land of Israel into the hands of our enemies. And so he wrote in his introduction: "Now, when Jewish sovereignty over the Temple Mount is in danger, Mount Moriah is liable to become a subject of negotiation between us and the Arabs; and to our sorrow there are politicians who are ready to negotiate over our sovereignty over the Temple Mount, and they rely on the supposed prohibition of the rabbinate to go up onto the Temple Mount. This prohibition is liable to serve as a pretext for handing over the holy of holies of the nation into the hands of the Muslims. Therefore I decided to publish the book now, from which they will see that there are extensive areas on the Temple Mount permitted for entry to every Jew according to all opinions, after he immerses in a pure mikve…" (p. 15).

The reasons for the permissive ruling

On the Temple Mount there are two parts. One, the smaller, includes the place of the Temple and the courtyards and is called the camp of the Shekhina. It is forbidden to enter it in our days, because we cannot purify ourselves from the impurity of the dead. The second, which is most of the area of the Temple Mount, is called the Levite camp, and it is permitted to enter it in our days after immersion. Indeed, it is known that in the years before the establishment of the State the rabbis, among them Maran Ha-Rav Kook zt"l, ruled not to go up onto the whole Temple Mount, out of concern lest people go across and enter the forbidden places too.

Three reasons moved Rav Goren to permit going up to most of the area of the Temple Mount:

(a) The precise mapping of the Temple Mount carried out by the Engineering Corps at his instruction after the liberation of the Temple Mount – maps according to which it was possible to determine with certainty where the places permitted for entry according to all opinions are.

(b) The many testimonies that for more than a thousand years after the destruction the great ones of Israel were accustomed to pray on the Temple Mount in the permitted places.

(c) The threat to Jewish sovereignty on the Temple Mount.

There is room to add that it is possible that one of the motives for setting up the warning signs not to go up onto the Mount in the days of Rav Kook was so as not to provoke the Muslims and the rulers who then ruled the Land, who at times of riots did not properly protect the Jews.

The descent to the Wall – a result of the sufferings of exile

Rav Goren wrote about his feelings after the Six-Day War: "I could not free myself from the feeling that, historically, the dedication of the Western Wall plaza to Jewish prayer is nothing but a result of the expulsion of the Jews from the Temple Mount by the Crusaders and the Muslims alike. Thus an unbearable situation was created in which, even after the liberation of the Temple Mount by us, the Muslims remained on the Temple Mount above and we below, they inside and we outside. The prayers by the Western Wall are a symbol of destruction and exile and not of liberation and redemption, for the prayers of the Jews by the Western Wall began only in the sixteenth century; before that the Jews prayed for hundreds of years on the Temple Mount… and only about three hundred years ago did the Jews begin to pray by the Western Wall. And let it be known that wherever it is mentioned in the Midrash that the Shekhina did not move from the Western Wall – learning this from the verse in Shir Ha-Shirim, 'Behold, he stands behind our wall' – the intention is the western wall of the Azara or of the Heikhal, which is the wall of the Holy of Holies, and not of the Temple Mount, which is our Western Wall" (p. 26).

* *

The need to go up from the Western Wall to the Temple Mount

However, the force of a custom that was established over three hundred years is great, and therefore after the Six-Day War the broad public streamed to pray at the Western Wall. Rav Goren himself also wrote that one of the things that prevented him from hastening to arrange going up onto the Temple Mount was his being "bound with cords of love to the remnant of our Temple, the Western Wall, where I was accustomed to pray every Shabbat and festival and on the eves of Rosh Ḥodesh. Since my first visit to the Western Wall (as a child) my love and spiritual attachment to the Wall of Tears has not faded…", "but the voice of the cry… 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord…'" roused him to strengthen himself and clarify the permission to go up onto the Temple Mount (p. 14). And therefore he began to organise prayers on the Temple Mount (there, p. 27).

The prayer that was cancelled

Towards Shabbat Naḥamu 5727 Rav Goren announced that a festive mass prayer would be held on the Temple Mount, in the area permitted for entry after immersion. However, by instruction of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence the prayer was cancelled. A few days later a ministerial committee decided that the Minister of Defence and the Chief of Staff would instruct the Chief Rabbi of the IDF, Rav Goren, not to organise any more prayers on the Temple Mount (pp. 29-30).

The shock

The instruction shocked Rav Goren, and he tried to cancel it with all his ability, including writing a long and reasoned letter to the ministerial committee, in which he argued: how can it be that precisely in the holiest place for Jews it should be forbidden for Jews to pray?! Indeed there are limited places into which entry is forbidden by the Torah to Jews and gentiles alike, but the great majority of the Temple Mount is permitted for entry. Towards the end of his letter he called out: "Distinguished personalities! Save the holy of holies of the nation; do not hand over the Temple Mount into the hands of its desecrators…" (pp. 30-33).

The Minister of Defence

To our sorrow, Rav Goren's call was not answered. The Minister of Defence Moshe Dayan decided to transfer responsibility for managing the arrangements of the Temple Mount to the Waqf, and ordered the military rabbinate to vacate the Temple Mount and no longer to interfere in any matter whatsoever concerning the Temple Mount. Rav Goren responded "with fury and sorrow", and informed the Minister of Defence "that this is liable to bring, heaven forbid, the destruction of the Third Temple, since the key to our rule over Judea, Samaria and the Gaza region is the Temple Mount" (p. 34).

However, the Minister of Defence carried out one of the most shameful acts in the history of Israel and handed over the management of the affairs of the Temple Mount to the Muslim Waqf. For years it was known that Moshe Dayan had two sides. Darkness and light functioned in him intermingled. On the one hand a hero of Israel, and on the other an adulterer and a thief. Apparently his adulteries and thefts tipped the scales against him. In this matter his name will be remembered with abhorrence.

Sovereignty

Indeed, after the Muslims closed the Mughrabi Gate in order to prevent the entry of Jews onto the Mount, at Rav Goren's request the IDF broke open the gate in order to ensure free entry for Jews, and thereby expressed sovereignty over the Temple Mount. However, this act did not change the instruction that forbade the prayer of Jews on the Temple Mount.

Rav Goren continues and relates: "Whenever I warned against handing over the holy of holies of the Jewish nation to the Waqf, the answer of the heads of government in all periods was: in any case the Chief Rabbinate forbids Jews to go up onto the Temple Mount, and we are prevented from praying there." Following this he decided to write the book and to explain the ways, the places and the conditions in which it is permitted to go up onto the Temple Mount (p. 35). Therefore "one must exhaust all the aspects of permission, so that we may be able to demonstrate a constant Jewish presence there and guard Jewish sovereignty over the Mount like the apple of our eye" (p. 46).

The rabbinate's sign

There are those who claim that Rav Goren, during his term as Chief Rabbi, agreed to the prohibition of entering the Temple Mount, but the truth is not so. In the introduction to his book he wrote: "During the period of my term as Chief Rabbi of Israel, I brought a proposal to the Council of the Chief Rabbinate to take down the signs prohibiting going up onto the Mount, which the Chief Rabbis who preceded me had set up. Since among the members of the council there were some who had at the time signed the prohibition, they asked to postpone the decision to take down the signs prohibiting going up onto the Temple Mount until I published the book…". For various reasons the publication of the book was postponed, and the signs remained in place, "something that caused the actual handing over of the Temple Mount to the Muslim Waqf" (there, p. 35).

Desecration of the holy

Moreover he wrote: "This shameful situation, in which under the rule of Israel a Jew has no right of prayer on the Mount of the Lord, must not be accepted in any way whatsoever. The debate over where it is permitted according to halakha to go up onto the Temple Mount and where it is forbidden does not concern the government… These sanctified places are not the private property of the Muslim Waqf, whose members have always been a root bearing gall and wormwood for the Jews, inciting from within the mosques on the Temple Mount to carry out massacres of Jews… Had they closed the Temple Mount to Jews and non-Jews alike, I would have kept silent; but to allow the Arabs to do there as if it were their own, and to forbid Jews to open a book of Tehillim there and pour out their hearts before the Creator of the world – this is a religious, historical and legal scandal bordering on desecration of the holy!" (p. 41).

He further added (p. 42): by refraining from going up onto the Temple Mount one transgresses the Torah prohibition of 'lo teḥonem' – do not give them a resting place in the land (Avoda Zara 20a), for the poskim have already established that the loss of sovereignty is like destruction (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham OḤ 561:1). It follows that when the government forbids Jews to go up freely, it destroys again the place of our Temple.

Blessed are those who go up

The continuation of the shameful situation on the Temple Mount breathes hope into our enemies and moves them to murders and riots throughout the Land. In order to strangle the wave of terror and incitement at its root, the government and the police must express in the most decisive way the sovereignty of Israel over the Temple Mount. Blessed are those who go up onto the Temple Mount according to halakha. In their merit our sovereignty over the Mount and over the whole Land of Israel is made clear, and precisely through this we will merit security and peace.
